heading: Introduction
text:
INTRODUCTION
Nursing assessment is the systematic collection and analysis of relevant data about a patient's physical, psychological, sociocultural, and spiritual health status, using various assessment techniques and tools (Jarvis, 2020). Assessment is the first step of the nursing process. It involves the systematic collection of data about the individual’s health status, abilities and any actual and potential health problems. The data can be obtained from the patient, relatives, literature review and diagnostic investigations. Assessment is done through inspection, diagnostic investigation, percussion, palpation and auscultation.
Patient Particulars
Patient particulars refer to identifying information such as the patient's full name, date of birth, gender, address, contact details, and any unique identifiers used in healthcare records (Jarvis 2020). It is done by asking the patient if he/she is able or a relative to help give a holistic care.. Mrs. T.T is a 54 year old woman born on 12th June, 1969 at Sunyani municipal hospital to the late Mr. A.S and Mrs. A.S. She is the second born of the four children of her parents which are all currently alive and doing well. She is a window with two children of which all are females. She together with her two children lives in Yawhima a community in Sunyani and their house number is YH81/3. Seikwa, a village in Tain district of Bono Region is the name of her hometown and is seamstress by profession. She speaks and communicates well in Bono language. Mrs. T.T is fair in complexion, 1.56m tall and 55kg heavy during admission. Junior high school is the highest level of education she has attained and could not further due to economic insufficiency. Mr. P.O is her chosen next of kin who is the second daughter. She is Christian and worships at Apostles Continuation Church International at Sunyani.
Patients/Family Medical History
According to Mrs. T.T, apart from her older sister who is currently suffering from diabetes mellitus, she has not learned about any known familial disease condition nor witnessed any mental illness amongst her family. Mrs. T.T grandparents are late and had a natural cause of their death even though her mother died as a result of breast cancer. Her father and husband also died through a road traffic accident. Nevertheless, the other siblings of hers are alive and doing well without any health condition. However, she explained that her family sometimes experience minor symptoms such as cough, fever, and headache of which they manage at home with over the counter drugs. Mrs. T.T is not aware of any allergic reaction to food and drug.
Patients Socioeconomic History
Mrs. T.T is a seamstress which is her major source of income. She relates absolutely well with her siblings and children who are always economically, psychologically and emotionally supportive. Her first daughter is a midwife, who also financially supports her when in need. She strengthens and maintains her social relationships by attending and participating in weddings, funerals and other social gatherings of concerns. Her estimated average total income per month is around GH₵1500 when calculated.
Patients Developmental History
Human development refers to the qualitative and continuous enhancement in physical, cognitive, emotional, and social features and abilities and that individuals experience from birth through old age (Santrock, 2022). Human growth refers to the progressive and measurable physical changes that occur over an individual's lifespan, including height, weight, bone development, and other physiological aspects (Santrock, 2022). Maturation refers specifically to the biologically driven process of aging and physical growth, including the development of structures and functions within an organism. It encompasses genetically programmed changes that occur naturally over time, leading to increased biological complexity and functionality (Tanner et al, 2021). Mrs. T.T underwent spontaneous vaginal delivery without any labor inducing medication given neither did her mother have any difficulties during delivery. She was vaccinated against the vaccine preventable diseases hence, she did not suffer from any childhood disease that could have impaired her development and growth. Mrs. T.T was able to sit when she was five months old and developed milk teeth by the sixth month. She could crawl around the 7th months and started to walk when she was 12th months old even though she was not exclusively breastfed. Mrs. T.T started her basic education at age six and completed when she was 17. She aspired to become a medical doctor but couldn’t attain that due lack of support financially during her schooling tenure. Mrs. T.T begun to experience secondary sexual characteristics by age 15 and her menopausal symptoms developed around the 46th year of her life. Erik Erickson’s theory of psychosocial development includes the following stages;
Trust versus mistrust (birth to 18months)
Autonomy versus shame and doubt (18months to 3years)
Initiative versus guilt (3 to 5years)
Industry versus inferiority (6 to 11years)
Identity versus role confusion (12 to 18years)
Intimacy versus isolation (18 to 40years)
Generativity versus stagnation (40 to 65years)
Integrity versus despair (65 to death)
Comparing her age with Erik Erikson’s psychosocial theory, she falls under generativity versus stagnation which is the seventh stage and rages from 40 to 65 years. According to Erikson, those who are successful in this stage feel productive and have been able to contribute to their family and the society whilst those who are not successful feel that have failed to be productive to their society. Mrs. T.T has been able to nurture her children to also become responsible adults, acquire belongings and possession for herself, able to pay taxes and partake in community developmental programs and this apparently confirms that she is successful at this stage and eligibly makes her generative.
Lifestyle/ Hobbies
According to her, mostly, she wakes up around 4:00am and takes a word of prayer before getting out of bed. From there she observes her personal hygiene which includes brushing of teeth, taking her shower and emptying her bowels. Also, she performs some other general house chores including, sweeping the compound, washing dishes and cooking. Normally, she goes to work during weekdays at 7:30am and closes at 5:30pm and sometimes attends church, weddings and funeral activities during the weekends. She is capable of feeding, grooming, dressing and walking conveniently without difficulties. Mrs. T.T does not indulge in smoking, drinking, or consume any form of drug or stimulants. Mrs. T.T eliminates her bladder at least three times daily and bowels once daily mostly before taking her bath. She mostly takes porridge as her breakfast, rice and vegetable stew for lunch and fufu and light soup for supper for her three square meals. She is able to have enough sleep and rest without any challenge or use of sleeping pills and usually goes to bed at 9:00pm and wakes up at 4:00am. She has not identified any allergic reaction to either food or drug. She is a mother and plays the expected roles and responsibilities accordingly. She is fond of reading the scripture oftentimes and is a mere member of the church she worships at. She is sociable and the free type.
Past Medical History
Mrs. T.T ever suffered from chills and fever which when she reported to the hospital and was diagnosed of malaria and was provided with antimalarial medications to take home for treatment. She never suffered any childhood illness such as measles and diphtheria neither has she sustained any serious injuries or road traffic accidents in her life. Before the advent of her current condition, she had never been hospitalized due any illness or disease. She has no physical disability. She sometime purchases and uses pain medications and cold relievers from pharmacy and drugs stores nearby to treat minor ailments such headache, catarrh and fever. Yawhima health center is the closest health facility to her and sometimes visits there for medical and obstetric care. Mrs. T.T experienced her menarche at 15 and has had consistent menstrual flow monthly with no complications. She has had two deliveries out of the two pregnancies in her life time which all her two deliveries were through spontaneous vaginal delivery. Mrs. T.T has never used any contraceptives nor aborted any pregnancy before.
Present Medical History
According to Mrs. T.T she was strong and healthy until 18th August, 2023, when she begun to experience sudden symptoms including palpitation, dizziness, fatigue, headache and general body weakness which led to her visitation and eventually hospitalization to the facility.
Admission Of Patient
On the 18th of August, 2023, Mrs. T.T came to the female medical ward through the emergency and accident unit accompanied by a nurse and a relative in a wheelchair at 7:30pm. She was warmly welcomed, attended to and introduced to the ward. An admission bed was prepared for her to rest. Vital signs were checked and recorded as;
Temperature - 26.7°C,
Pulse – 82bpm,
Respiration – 22cpm and
Blood pressure - 200/160mmhg.
Oxygen saturation rate – 95%
A thorough orientation about ward routines that is medication time; (6:00am, 10:00am, 2:00pm, 6:00pm and 10:00pm), meal times (breakfast; 7:30am, lunch; 12:30pm and supper; 5:30pm) and visiting hours (5:30am – 6:00am and 4:30pm), ward surroundings and also introduced her to other patients she was going to share the same cubicle with. A thorough and complete physical assessment was carried out and findings include; palpitation, dizziness, fatigue, headache and general body weakness. The diagnostic investigations ordered to be carried out include; lipid profile and creatinine test. From the report her diagnosis was hypertension and initial treatment given was tab Nefidipine 60mg stat at 7:35pm while subsequent treatment that would continue were;
Tab Nefidipine 30mg bd x30 days
Tab Losartan 100mg od x  7 days
Tab hydralazine 50mg tds x 5 days
IV Mannitol 300mls tds x 3 days
Tab paracetamol 1g tid x 7 days
Mrs. T.T and her family were expected to participate and collaborate in the holistic care given to her by providing suitable and best responds to all they will be asked of. There after I attended to her and discussed with her the possibility and the consensus about employing her to be my patient for a project called care study which she totally agreed to and collaborated during collection of data and throughout the whole project.
Patient Concept Of Illness
Mrs. T.T revealed that she is anxious of the outcome of the condition; however she did not relate the cause of the condition to any spiritual background since she believes hypertension is normal medical condition which can be acquired by humans. Also she was afraid of losing her customer to other seamstresses due to the conception that treatment may delay but hoped she gets well as soon as possible so she can resume work and perform other relevant activities at home. She had faith that God is capable of everything and believed that He is going to provide her with instant recovery and strength plus good health against the disease. I then saw it an opportunity and took it to elaborate her through the condition, causes, some signs and symptoms of hypertension and lifestyles that will aggravates and mitigate the condition.
Literature Review Of Hypertension
Definition Of Hypertension
Hypertension (high blood pressure) is occurs when the pressure exerted on your blood vessels by the streaming blood is higher than normal (140/90 mmHg or higher) (WHO, 2023). It is a chronic medical condition characterized by elevated blood pressure levels in the arteries. It is a significant risk factor for various cardiovascular diseases and can lead to serious health complications if left untreated.
Incidence Of Hypertension
According to the World Health Organization;
Hypertension is a major cause of premature death worldwide.
It is more common in adults of age 30–79years
It affects majorly people living in low- and middle-income countries.
Classification Of Hypertension
Normal: SBP < 120 mm hg and DBP < 80 mm hg
Elevated: SBP 120-129 mm hg and DBP < 80 mm hg
Hypertension stage 1: SBP 130-139 mm hg or DBP 80-89 mm hg
Hypertension stage 2: SBP ≥ 140 mm hg or DBP ≥ 90 mm hg
Hypertensive crisis: SBP > 180 mm hg and/or DBP > 120 mm hg
Types Of Hypertension
Primary/essential hypertension: Primary hypertension is the most common type and occurs when there is no specific identifiable cause for high blood pressure. It tends to develop gradually over time and is often related to a combination of genetic, lifestyle, and aging factors.
Secondary hypertension: Secondary hypertension occurs as a result of an underlying medical condition or medication side effects. It is typically more abrupt in onset than primary hypertension and may develop at any age.
Other types of hypertension include
Resistant hypertension: Resistant hypertension is diagnosed when a person's blood pressure remains high despite taking multiple antihypertensive medications at maximal doses. It may require additional evaluation and treatment adjustments.
Isolated Systolic Hypertension: Isolated Systolic Hypertension is characterized by elevated systolic blood pressure (the top number) with normal diastolic blood pressure. It is more common in older adults and is often related to stiffening of the arteries.
Malignant hypertension: Malignant hypertension is a severe and rapidly progressive form of high blood pressure. It can lead to organ damage and requires immediate medical attention.
Predisposing Factors Of Hypertension
Genetics (Non-Modifiable)
Family history
Age
Gender
Environmental (Modifiable)
Stress
Occupation
Socioeconomic status
Nutrition
Obesity
Lifestyle/habit
Causes Of Secondary Hypertension
Kidney Disease:
Renal Artery Stenosis: Narrowing of the renal arteries that supply blood to the kidneys can lead to increased blood pressure. This can result from atherosclerosis or fibromuscular dysplasia.
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): Kidney damage or dysfunction can disrupt the regulation of blood pressure, leading to hypertension.
Hormonal Disorders:
Primary Aldosteronism (Conn's Syndrome): Overproduction of aldosterone hormone by the adrenal glands can cause sodium and water retention, leading to high blood pressure.
Cushing's syndrome: Excessive production of cortisol, often due to adrenal tumors, can elevate blood pressure.
Pheochromocytoma: A rare adrenal gland tumor that produces excess catecholamines, causing sudden and severe spikes in blood pressure.
Hyperthyroidism: Overactive thyroid glands can raise blood pressure.
Obstructive Sleep Apnea (OSA):
OSA is a sleep disorder characterized by interruptions in breathing during sleep. It is associated with hypertension, likely due to repeated episodes of oxygen deprivation and increased sympathetic nervous system activity.
Cardiovascular disease:
Coarctation of the aorta: A congenital heart defect where the aorta narrows, restricting blood flow and causing high blood pressure in the arms while blood pressure remains low in the legs.
Myocardia infarction
Valvular stenosis
Endocrine Disorders:
Other endocrine disorders, such as acromegaly, hyperparathyroidism, and congenital adrenal hyperplasia, can contribute to secondary hypertension.
Neurological Conditions:
Conditions affecting the brain or central nervous system, such as brain tumors, head injuries, or conditions that affect the hypothalamus or pituitary gland, can lead to hypertension.
Pregnancy-Induced Hypertension:
Conditions like preeclampsia or gestational hypertension can develop during pregnancy and lead to elevated blood pressure. These typically resolve after delivery but require monitoring and management during pregnancy.
Illegal Drug Use:
The use of substances like cocaine or amphetamines can result in acute and severe increases in blood pressure.
Adrenal Disorders:
Conditions affecting the adrenal glands, such as adenomas or hyperplasia, can disrupt the normal balance of hormones and lead to hypertension.
Pathophysiology Of Hypertension
The human body is made up of network of arteries and other blood vessels, responsible for delivering oxygen and nutrients to every cell, tissue and organ of the human body. The constant flow of blood relies on a delicate balance between pressure and resistance. Under normal circumstances, the walls of these vessels are flexible and elastic, allowing them to expand and contract as needed, maintaining stable blood pressure. However, when the balance of this system is disrupted, hypertension begins to develop. Over time, the blood vessels become stiff and less responsive. This increased arterial stiffness raises the resistance against the force of blood flow, forcing the heart to pump harder. This constant strain on the heart not only tires it but also sets the stage for a steady increase in blood pressure levels. Renin-Angiotensin-Aldosterone System (RAAS) is a hormone system and critical regulator of fluid and electrolyte balance and blood pressure found in the kidneys. When the kidneys sense a drop in blood flow or sodium levels, they release renin, an enzyme that initiates a series of events. Renin activates angiotensinogen, a precursor protein, converting it into angiotensin I, which is then transformed into the villainous angiotensin II. This angiotensin II character is a master of vasoconstriction, causing blood vessels to constrict and narrow, thereby increasing blood pressure. Moreover, it signals the adrenal glands to release aldosterone, a hormone that prompts the retention of sodium and water, further boosting blood pressure. As blood pressure elevates within the arteries, another sinister player enters the scene—endothelial dysfunction. The inner lining of the blood vessels acts as a protective barrier. These endothelial cells are responsible for producing nitric oxide (NO), a powerful vasodilator that helps keep blood vessels relaxed and open. In hypertension, chronic inflammation and oxidative stress damage these cells, reducing producing nitric oxide availability and causing the blood vessels to lose their ability to relax. This results in a prolonged vasoconstriction and increased vascular resistance, contributing to higher blood pressure. Also In hypertension, the sympathetic nervous system goes haywire, releasing torrents of norepinephrine, a stress hormone which eventually ramps up your heart rate, increases cardiac output, and tightens blood vessels, making them narrower and more resistant conspiring to the elevation of blood pressure, pushing it to dangerous levels (WHO, 2023).
Signs And Symptoms Of Hypertension
Hypertension, often referred to as the "silent killer," typically doesn't present obvious signs or symptoms until it reaches advanced stages or causes complications. However, some people with extremely high blood pressure may experience specific signs and symptoms such as;
Headaches: Severe headaches, often described as pounding or pulsating, can occur with high blood pressure. However, headaches are a non-specific symptom and can have various causes.
Fatigue and Weakness: Some individuals with hypertension may feel unusually tired or weak, especially if their high blood pressure is severe and affecting organ function.
Vision Problems: Hypertensive retinopathy, a condition where high blood pressure damages the blood vessels in the eyes, can lead to vision changes or blurred vision.
Chest Pain: In cases of extremely high blood pressure, individuals may experience chest pain or discomfort, which can mimic symptoms of angina or heart attack. This is a medical emergency.
Shortness of Breath: Hypertension can lead to fluid accumulation in the lungs, causing shortness of breath, especially during physical exertion or lying flat.
Dizziness or Vertigo: Some people with high blood pressure may experience dizziness, lightheadedness, or vertigo (a spinning sensation). These symptoms can be especially pronounced when moving from a sitting to a standing position.
Nosebleeds: While not a common symptom, persistent or severe nosebleeds may be associated with hypertension. Nosebleeds are usually more prevalent in cases of extremely high blood pressure.
Chest Congestion: Hypertension can contribute to heart failure, leading to symptoms like chest congestion, coughing, and swelling in the legs and ankles.Top of Form
Palpitations: Palpitation is a common symptom experienced by major hypertensive patients due to increased workload of the heart and peripheral resistance.
Diagnostic Investigations Of Hypertension
Diagnosing hypertension involves a series of blood pressure monitoring to determine if an individual has consistently elevated blood pressure levels. Additionally, further differential diagnostic tests may be conducted to identify any underlying causes of secondary hypertension. Here are some actual and subsequent differential diagnostic investigations conducted for hypertension:
Actual Diagnostic Investigations:
Blood Pressure Measurement:
The primary diagnostic test for hypertension is the measurement of blood pressure. It's essential to use a calibrated and appropriately sized blood pressure cuff. Blood pressure readings should be taken on multiple occasions to confirm the diagnosis.
Ambulatory Blood Pressure Monitoring (ABPM):
ABPM involves wearing a portable device that measures blood pressure at regular intervals over a 24-hour period. It provides a more accurate assessment of blood pressure patterns than isolated office measurements.
Home Blood Pressure Monitoring:
Patients can monitor their blood pressure at home using home blood pressure monitors. Regular monitoring can help healthcare professionals assess overall blood pressure control and response to treatment.
Differential Diagnostic Investigations (To Identify Secondary Causes):
Urinalysis: Urinalysis can help identify signs of kidney disease, such as proteinuria (protein in the urine) or hematuria (blood in the urine), which may indicate an underlying cause of hypertension.
Blood Tests: Blood tests may include measurements of serum creatinine, blood urea nitrogen (BUN), and electrolytes (e.g., sodium and potassium). Abnormalities in these values can suggest kidney dysfunction or hormonal imbalances.
Renal Imaging: Imaging studies like renal ultrasound, CT scans, or MRIs of the kidneys can help identify structural abnormalities or renal artery stenosis as potential causes of secondary hypertension.
Hormone Testing: Hormonal assessments can include measuring plasma renin activity, aldosterone levels, and thyroid function tests to rule out conditions like primary aldosteronism, hyperthyroidism, or pheochromocytoma.
Echocardiography: Echocardiography (ultrasound of the heart) can assess cardiac structure and function, helping to detect signs of hypertensive heart disease or other heart-related conditions.
Sleep Studies: Polysomnography or home sleep apnea testing may be conducted to diagnose obstructive sleep apnea, which is associated with hypertension in some cases.
Genetic Testing: Genetic testing may be considered if a genetic cause of hypertension is suspected based on family history or other clinical factors.
Lipid Profile: A lipid profile measures cholesterol levels in the blood and can help assess cardiovascular risk factors in individuals with hypertension.
Glucose Testing: Glucose testing, including fasting blood glucose or HbA1c levels, can help evaluate diabetes risk, which is closely associated with hypertension.
Inflammatory Markers: Some individuals with hypertension may undergo tests to assess inflammatory markers, as inflammation can play a role in the development of cardiovascular disease.
Medical Management Of A Hypertensive Patient
Medical management of a hypertensive patient aims to control blood pressure, reduce the risk of complications, and improve overall cardiovascular health. The approach may vary based on the severity of hypertension and the individual patient's needs. Here are some key components of medical management for hypertensive patients:
Lifestyle Modifications:
Dietary Changes: Encourage a heart-healthy diet that is low in sodium (salt), rich in fruits and vegetables, whole grains, lean proteins, and low-fat dairy products. This dietary approach, often referred to as the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet, helps lower blood pressure by reducing sodium intake and increasing potassium intake.
Physical Activity: Promote regular exercise, such as brisk walking, swimming, or cycling, for at least 150 minutes per week. Physical activity helps improve cardiovascular health and lowers blood pressure.
Weight Management: Encourage weight loss for overweight or obese patients, as excess weight can contribute to hypertension. Even modest weight loss can lead to significant blood pressure reductions.
Smoking Cessation: Assist patients in quitting smoking, as tobacco use can raise blood pressure and increase the risk of heart disease. Offer smoking cessation resources and support.
Limit Alcohol Intake: Advise moderation in alcohol consumption. Excessive alcohol can raise blood pressure and interfere with the effectiveness of antihypertensive medications.
Medications:
Antihypertensive Medications: Prescribe and adjust antihypertensive medications based on the patient's blood pressure readings, overall health, and any underlying conditions. Common classes of medications include:
Diuretics: Promote fluid and sodium excretion, reducing blood volume and pressure.
ACE Inhibitors: Relax blood vessels and decrease fluid retention.
ARBs (Angiotensin II Receptor Blockers): Block the effects of angiotensin II, a hormone that constricts blood vessels.
Beta-Blockers: Reduce heart rate and cardiac output.
Calcium Channel Blockers: Relax blood vessel walls and reduce cardiac workload.
Combination Therapy: In some cases, a combination of antihypertensive medications from different classes may be necessary to achieve blood pressure control.
Regular Medication Adherence: Emphasize the importance of taking medications as prescribed and monitor for side effects or interactions with other medications.
Blood Pressure Monitoring: Encourage regular monitoring of blood pressure at home, and instruct patients on how to record and report readings accurately.
Routine Follow-Up and Assessments: Schedule regular follow-up appointments to monitor blood pressure, assess the patient's response to treatment, and make necessary adjustments to the medication regimen.
Management of Comorbid Conditions: Address and manage other health conditions that may contribute to or worsen hypertension, such as diabetes or high cholesterol.
Emergency Preparedness: In severe cases of hypertension, educate patients about hypertensive emergencies and the importance of seeking immediate medical attention if they experience symptoms such as severe headaches, chest pain, shortness of breath, or neurological symptoms.
Education and Counseling: Provide patient education about the long-term consequences of untreated hypertension and the benefits of blood pressure control. Offer counseling on lifestyle modifications and medication adherence.
Cardiovascular Risk Assessment: Conduct a comprehensive assessment of cardiovascular risk factors, including cholesterol levels, diabetes, and family history, to tailor treatment strategies to the patient's overall risk profile.
Preventive Measures: Encourage preventive measures, such as vaccination against influenza and pneumonia, as well as aspirin therapy if indicated, to reduce the risk of cardiovascular events.
Nursing Management Of Hypertension
Psychological Care
Regularly assess the patient's emotional state, including stress levels, anxiety, and depression.
Educate the patient about hypertension, its risk factors, and the importance of blood pressure control
Teach stress reduction techniques such as deep breathing exercises, progressive muscle relaxation, or mindfulness meditation.
Offer emotional support by providing a compassionate and empathetic environment.
Help the patient set achievable goals for lifestyle modifications, such as dietary changes, exercise, and smoking cessation.
Connect patients with hypertension support groups or community resources where they can interact with others facing similar challenges.
Sleep and rest
Conduct a thorough assessment of the patient's sleep patterns and quality.
Collaborate with healthcare providers to identify and address sleep-related disorders, such as obstructive sleep apnea.
Teach stress reduction techniques, such as relaxation exercises, deep breathing, or meditation, to help the patient manage stress and anxiety that may interfere with sleep.
Advise the patient to limit fluid intake in the evening to reduce nighttime awakenings for bathroom trips, especially if they are taking diuretics.
Encourage the patient to keep a sleep diary to track their sleep patterns, including bedtime, wake time, and any disruptions.
Observations
Continuously monitor the patient's blood pressure as per the healthcare provider's orders and the institution's protocol. Record and document blood pressure readings accurately, noting any trends or significant fluctuations.
Perform regular vital signs assessments, including monitoring heart rate, respiratory rate, and temperature. Changes in vital signs can provide valuable information about the patient's overall condition and potential complications.
Be vigilant for signs and symptoms of hypertensive crisis, such as severe headaches, chest pain, shortness of breath, confusion, or neurological deficits.
Evaluate the patient for signs of target organ damage, including hypertensive retinopathy (eye changes), renal dysfunction, and cardiac symptoms such as chest pain or heart failure.
Monitor the patient for potential side effects or adverse reactions to antihypertensive medications including dizziness, orthostatic hypotension, electrolyte imbalances, and renal dysfunction.
Assess fluid status by monitoring daily weights and evaluating for signs of edema, particularly in the legs and ankles.
Nutrition
Begin with a thorough assessment of the patient's dietary habits, including their typical daily intake, meal patterns, and any specific dietary restrictions or preferences.
Educate the patient about the importance of a heart-healthy diet, such as the DASH (Dietary Approaches to Stop Hypertension) diet. Emphasize the following principles:
Low Sodium: Advise reducing sodium intake to less than 2,300 milligrams (mg) per day or lower, especially for individuals with high blood pressure.
High Potassium: Encourage foods rich in potassium, as it can help counteract the effects of sodium. Good sources include fruits (e.g., bananas, oranges), vegetables (e.g., potatoes, spinach), and beans.
Fruits and Vegetables: Promote a diet rich in fruits and vegetables, aiming for at least 5 servings per day.
Whole Grains: Encourage whole grains over refined grains (e.g., whole wheat bread instead of white bread).
Lean Proteins: Recommend lean protein sources like poultry, fish, beans, and tofu.
Limit Saturated and Trans Fats: Advise reducing saturated and trans fats, which can contribute to cardiovascular risk.
Teach the patient about appropriate portion sizes to prevent overeating, which can contribute to weight gain and hypertension.
Educate the patient on how to read food labels for sodium content and choose low-sodium or sodium-free alternatives when available. Encourage cooking at home to have better control over sodium levels.
Stress the importance of staying adequately hydrated with water, as dehydration can affect blood pressure. Limiting excessive caffeine and alcohol intake is also crucial.
Medications
Administer medications as prescribed, ensuring accurate dosing, route, and timing.
Continuously assess the patient for potential side effects or adverse reactions to antihypertensive medications.
Regularly evaluate the patient's adherence to their medication regimen. Address any concerns, barriers, or misconceptions about the medications and work collaboratively to resolve them.
Monitor the patient's blood pressure regularly to assess the effectiveness of the antihypertensive medications
Help the patient manage their medication supply by assisting with prescription refills, providing reminders, and ensuring they have an adequate stock of medications to avoid interruptions in treatment.
. Stress the importance of medication adherence and the need to continue taking medications even when feeling well. . Stress the importance of medication adherence and the need to continue taking medications even when feeling well.

Protection From Injury
Ensure that the patient's environment is safe by removing tripping hazards, securing rugs, and ensuring adequate lighting, especially in hallways and bathrooms.
Provide and encourage the use of assistive devices such as canes, walkers, or handrails to improve mobility and stability, especially if the patient is at high risk of falls.
Educate the patient about the risk of orthostatic hypotension (a sudden drop in blood pressure when changing positions) and advise them to rise slowly from sitting or lying positions. Monitor for signs of orthostatic hypotension.
Education
Explain what hypertension (high blood pressure) is, including the importance of blood pressure measurements and how it is diagnosed.
Discuss the risk factors for hypertension, which may include family history, diet, lifestyle, and underlying medical conditions.
Provide guidance on lifestyle changes that can help lower blood pressure, including dietary adjustments (e.g., reducing sodium intake, increasing potassium-rich foods), regular physical activity, smoking cessation, and moderating alcohol consumption.
Explain the role of antihypertensive medications, their names, dosages, and potential side effects.
Teach the patient how to use a home blood pressure monitor correctly. Provide instructions on recording and tracking blood pressure readings and when to report significant changes to their healthcare provider.
Emphasize the importance of regular follow-up appointments with healthcare providers for blood pressure checks and medication adjustments.
Discuss stress reduction techniques, such as deep breathing exercises, meditation, and mindfulness, as stress can contribute to elevated blood pressure.
Inform the patient about available resources and support groups, both in the healthcare setting and the community, where they can find additional guidance, encouragement, and emotional support.
Discuss strategies to help the patient remember to take their medications, such as using pill organizers, setting alarms, or involving a family member in medication management.
Prevention
Provide education and support for lifestyle modifications that can prevent or manage hypertension. Emphasize the importance of maintaining a healthy weight, adopting a balanced diet, engaging in regular physical activity, quitting smoking, and limiting alcohol intake.
Encourage regular home blood pressure monitoring and teach the patient how to track their blood pressure readings
Stress the importance of consistent medication adherence to maintain blood pressure control.
Offer ongoing dietary education and encourage the adoption of a heart-healthy diet
Complications Of Hypertension
Hypertension, if left uncontrolled or poorly managed, can lead to a range of serious complications affecting various organ systems. These complications are often the result of long-term elevated blood pressure, which places excessive stress on blood vessels and organs. Some common complications of hypertension include:
Cardiovascular Complications:
Heart Disease: Hypertension increases the risk of coronary artery disease, which can lead to angina (chest pain), heart attacks (myocardial infarctions), and heart failure.
Stroke: High blood pressure is a leading cause of ischemic strokes (caused by blocked blood vessels in the brain) and hemorrhagic strokes (caused by bleeding in the brain).
Aneurysms: Persistent high blood pressure can weaken the walls of blood vessels, leading to the formation of aneurysms, which are bulges in blood vessel walls. These can rupture and cause life-threatening bleeding.
Peripheral Artery Disease (PAD): Hypertension can reduce blood flow to the limbs, causing symptoms such as leg pain, poor wound healing, and an increased risk of limb amputation.
Kidney Complications:
Chronic Kidney Disease (CKD): Hypertension is a leading cause of CKD. It can damage the small blood vessels in the kidneys, leading to decreased kidney function over time.
End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD): Untreated or poorly managed hypertension can progress to ESRD, where the kidneys lose their ability to function, requiring dialysis or kidney transplantation.
Eye Complications:
Hypertensive Retinopathy: Elevated blood pressure can damage the blood vessels in the retina, leading to vision changes, retinal hemorrhages, and, in severe cases, vision loss.
Neurological Complications:
Cognitive Impairment: Long-standing hypertension is associated with cognitive decline and an increased risk of developing conditions like vascular dementia or Alzheimer's disease.
Hypertensive Encephalopathy: Severe hypertension can cause brain swelling, leading to symptoms such as confusion, seizures, and loss of consciousness. This is a medical emergency.
Vascular Complications:
Atherosclerosis: Hypertension accelerates the development of atherosclerosis, the buildup of plaque in arteries, which can lead to various complications, including heart attacks and strokes.
Peripheral Vascular Disease: Narrowed and damaged blood vessels due to hypertension can reduce blood flow to the extremities, leading to complications like gangrene.
Metabolic Complications:
Diabetes: Hypertension and diabetes often coexist, and the combination of these conditions increases the risk of cardiovascular complications.
Metabolic Syndrome: Hypertension is a component of metabolic syndrome, a cluster of risk factors (including obesity and high cholesterol) that increases the risk of heart disease and diabetes.
Pregnancy-Related Complications:
Preeclampsia: High blood pressure during pregnancy can lead to preeclampsia, a condition characterized by high blood pressure, organ damage, and potentially serious complications for both the mother and baby.
Validation Of Data
Validation of patient data is the rechecking and cleaning to verify the accuracy, consistency and completeness of data assembled for analysis or decision-making and patient care (Hady, 2023). This section aims at confirming the correctness and integrity of data collected from patient/ or family during the assessment phase. Validation of data collected was ensured by conducting diagnostic investigations to confirm some of the signs and symptoms exhibited and medical condition of Mrs. T.T. It can then be confidently pronounced that data collected about Mrs. T.T’s health was meticulously validated for subsequent management.

chapter: Chapter Four: Implementation
heading: Introduction
text:
Introduction
Nursing implementation involves the application of evidence-based interventions and the provision of hands-on care to address the patient's physical, emotional, and psychosocial needs (Ignatavicius et al, 2017).
Summary Of Actual Nursing Care Rendered To Mrs. T.T And Family
Delivery of nursing care to Mrs. T.t commenced right from the admission day that is 18th august, 2023 to 24th august, 2023 at the female medical ward of bono regional hospital. Patient and her family were comprehensively assessed for health problems, empathetically taking care of, educated on some vital information about hypertension and many other intervention summed and organized together to ensure her quick recovery and regain of optimal health. The following is the daily actual nursing care rendered to Mrs. T.T and family in summary.
Day of Admission (18th August, 2023)
On the 18th of August, 2023, Mrs. T.T came to the female medical ward through the emergency and accident unit accompanied by a nurse and a relative in a wheelchair at 7:30pm. She was warmly welcomed, attended to and introduced to the ward. An admission bed was prepared for her to rest. Vital signs were checked and recorded as;
Temperature - 26.7°C,
Pulse – 82bpm,
Respiration – 22cpm and
Blood pressure - 200/160mmhg.
Oxygen saturation rate – 95%
A thorough orientation about ward routines thus, medication time; (6:00am, 10:00am, 2:00pm, 6:00pm and 10:00pm), meal times (breakfast; 7:30am, lunch; 12:30pm and supper; 5:30pm) and visiting hours (5:30am – 6:00am and 5:30pm) were done. Ward surroundings and other patients she was going to share the same cubicle with were also introduced to her. Thereafter I attended to her and discussed with her the possibility and her consensus about employing her to be my patient for a project called care study which she totally agreed to and collaborated during data collection and throughout the whole project. A thorough and complete physical assessment was carried out and findings include; palpitation, dizziness, fatigue, headache and general body weakness. The diagnostic investigations ordered to be carried out include; lipid profile and creatinine test. From the report her diagnosis was hypertension and the initial treatment given was tab Nefidipine 60mg stat at 7:35pm while subsequent treatment that would continue were;
Tab Nefidipine 30mg bd x 30 days
Tab Losartan 100mg od x  7 days
Tab hydralazine 50mg tds x 5 days
IV Mannitol 300mls tds   x 3 days
Tab paracetamol 1g tid x 7 days
Mrs. T.T and her family were expected to participate and collaborate in the holistic care given to her by providing suitable and best responds to all they will be asked of and can also ask questions for clarification. An intravenous line was set to collect blood sample for investigation and intravenous therapy.
At 8:00pm, Mrs. T.T complained of dizziness, an objective of dizziness relief and fall prevention were set to be achieved throughout the time she stays at the ward. To attain this goal, bed wheels were locked to avoid skidding of the bed to cause her to fall. Side rails of her bed were raised to protect her from falling off. She was also assisted in performing basic self-care activities such as bathing, ambulation and others. Prescribed tab Nefidipine was administered to tackle and obliterate dizziness as a result high blood pressure.
At 9:30pm, Mrs. T.T complained of severe headache after assessment, an objective was set to eliminate pain from patient within the next 24 hours. The interventions carried out were; the intensity of pain was assessed using the numeric pain rating scale which rating of 8/10 was recorded.  She was provided with diversional therapy by engaging her in an interesting conversation. Again, she was encouraged to have enough rest, wrapped ice cubes was applied to her forehead to relieve headache. Blood pressure was monitored four hourly to early detect and intervene abnormally increasing blood pressure. Tab paracetamol 1g was administered to relieve headache.
At 9:45pm Mrs. T.T appeared anxious, when she was asked she clearly stated she does not know if she can regain her wellbeing after treatment, thereafter, an objective to relief her anxiety was set to be achieved within the next 24 hours. Appropriate nursing interventions carried out were; Patient/family was reassured that she will regain good health with appropriate interventions, Every procedure carried on the patient was explained, All question asked by patient and relatives were tactfully and honestly answered, Patient/family were encouraged to allay all fears and concern about condition and treatment and Patient was informed hypertension get worse with stress and overthinking
Due medications were served and vital signs were checked and recorded at 10:00pm. She was then assisted to the washroom to take her bath and went to bed at 10:45pm. All procedures were documented and signed.
Second Day Of Admission (19th August, 2023)
Mrs. T.T woke up at 5:30am, she was assisted to the washroom to eliminate her bowels and take her bath after brushing her teeth. Her bed was re-laid appropriately with a clean bed linen to ensure her comfort. She took milo with Ideal milk and bread as her breakfast. At 6:00am, medications were administered and vital signs were checked and recorded as;
Blood pressure: 160/110 mmHg
Pulse rate: 84 bpm
Temperature: 36.7°C
Respiration: 22Cpm
Spo2: 96%
It was realized on this day that, Mrs. T.T could not sleep in the night through a conversation we had at 9:00am. A regain of an appreciable amount and quality of sleep as an objective was set to be achieved within 48 hours. The developed nursing interventions to combat the insomnia were; Patient was told that, proper measures would be put in place to enhance her sleep, simple bed without creases and crumps was provided to her, a quiet environment was ensured, Patient was assisted to take warm bath before going to bed and Visitors were restricted during sleeping hours.
At 10:00am due medications were administered and vitals were checked and recorded. Mrs. TT was given apple and banana which her elder daughter brought during visiting hours with her two other siblings. She appeared cheerful and interacted with them happily. Mrs. T.T was asked about the headache she complained of last night, which she clearly stated that, “I do not feel the headache anymore thanks to our wonderful interventions put in place”. As goal to relieve her of the headache was set on 18th august, 2023 at 9:30pm to be achieved within the next 24hours, it could be confirmed that, indeed it was fully met.
Since Mrs. T.T could hardly perform basic activities of daily living herself, a nursing diagnosis of activity intolerance related to general body weakness was formulated at 11:00am, an objective to aid her perform these activities was set to be achieved in the next 48 hours. Applicable nursing interventions implemented to achieve this goal were; patient nutritional status was assessed with BMI, patient was educated on nutritional meals available, patient was assisted to groom herself every morning, patient was encourage to do best they can, rest schedules were developed for patient, Patient was engaged in performing range of motion exercise and assistive devices like walkers were provided to patient to ambulate.  At 12:00 pm, Mrs. TT was served with rice and beans stew with fried fish as lunch. After eating her meal, she was assisted by her daughter to ambulate around the ward. Afterwards, she made comfortable in bed to have a bed rest. Later in the evening, Mrs. TT, was served with fufu with light soup and chicken for supper. She was able to eat two-third of the meal served. After that, she was assisted to the washroom to take shower.
At 6:00pm, prescribed medications were served and vital signs were checked and recorded after which I discussed with Mrs. TT my intention to visit her house the following day. At 10:00pm, all due prescribed medications were administered whilst vital signs were also checked and recorded after which she went to bed around 10:15pm. All procedures and interventions carried on her were documented and signed.
Third Day Of Admission (20th August, 2023)
Mrs. TT woke up around 5:15am; she was assisted to maintain her personal hygiene by brushing her teeth, eliminating her bowel and taking her bath. Her bed lining and cloths were changed to provide comfort. She was served with wheat with milk and bread for breakfast. 6:00am vital signs were checked and recorded as;
Blood Pressure: 150/90mmHg
Pulse: 90bpm
Temperature: 36.6°C
Respiration: 20cpm
Spo2: 98
At 7:30am, Mrs. T.T was diagnosed of risk for ineffective peripheral tissue perfusion related to increased peripheral resistance because of the abnormal increased in her blood pressure, an objective to maintain the a normal peripheral tissue perfusion was set to be achieved throughout the period of hospitalization. The set of interventions implemented to attain this goal were; Peripheral pulses, capillary refill, skin color, and temperature were regularly assessed to monitor changes in tissue perfusion, Patient's extremities were elevated as appropriate to reduce venous stasis and improve blood flow, Blood pressure was continuously monitored for any significant changes, Patient was encouraged and assisted with mobility, such as regular ambulation to prevent venous stasis and promote circulation, Patient was educated about risk factors for impaired tissue perfusion, including smoking, obesity, and sedentary lifestyle, Prescribed Tab hydralazine 50mg was administered to improve peripheral blood flow. On 24th August, 2023, Mrs. T.T had no digital clubbing and a capillary refill time less than 3sec during her discharge; therefore goal was fully met when evaluated.
At 11:45am, during interaction, it was found that, patient and family had little knowledge on disease condition. Upon assessment, a nursing diagnosis of knowledge deficit related to inadequate exposure to information about hypertension was formulated. An objective was set to help the patient acquire sufficient knowledge about the condition within six hours. Interventions carried out include the following; Client and relatives were assured that all discussions will be confidential, level of understanding of client and relatives was assessed by asking them questions about hypertension, adequate amount of information about hypertension was given to patient and family, a text literature of hypertension was provided to patient and relatives and Patient and relatives were encouraged to ask questions. During the review with her physician, it was requested that, she still stays in the ward for further management and observation. No treatment was added.
At 12:20 pm, Mrs. TT was served with jollof rice and egg for lunch and she was encouraged to empty the plate. Due medications were served and 2pm vital signs were checked and recorded in the nurses note. Mrs. TT was encouraged to have a bed rest by ensuring a quite environment. Banku with okro stew and beef was served at 4:45 as super. The objective set to help Mrs. T.T and family to gain adequate knowledge on hypertension was evaluated at 5:00pm and goal was fully met as nurse scored patient/family 8/10 in the post test conducted for them. Again, she was assisted to take a warm bath. At 10:00pm, all due medications were administered and vital signs were checked and recorded. She fell asleep around 10:25pm; documentations were done for all procedures.
Day Four Of Admission (21th August, 2023)
Mrs. T.t woke up at 6:00am, and looked impressively stronger as compared to previously, she could now perform self-care activities with ease. Before I got to the ward, Mrs. TT had already brushed her teeth and taken her bath, groomed herself and her bed lining was changed. Objective that was set to aid her regain her normal sleep pattern on 19th August, 2023 was evaluated at 6am which was fully met as she verbalized that, she had had improved amount and quality of sleep the previous days. She was served with rice porridge and bread as breakfast. Vital signs were checked and recorded as;
Blood Pressure: 140/80mmHg
Pulse: 81bpm
Temperature: 36.2°C
Respiration: 22cpm
Spo2: 98
Mrs. T.t had some bed rest after checking her vitals signs for about 30-45munites, after which she was encouraged to continue to comply to treatment and lifestyle modification in order to hasten her recovery.
At 9:00am, objective that was set to aid patient to perform basic activities of daily living and attain optimal personal hygiene on 19th August, 2023 was evaluated and goal was fully met as Mrs. T.T verbalized that she can now perform basic life activities with ease. Due medications were administered and vital signs were checked and recorded at 2:00pm after her lunch which was ampesi with palava sauce. Mrs. T.T showered at 6:30pm after she was visited by her pastor and sibling during visiting hours and finally went to at 10:30pm.
Day five Of Admission (22th August, 2023)
Mrs. T.t woke up around 5:45am with a massive improvement in her condition. She went to the washroom herself, performed all personal hygiene and came back safely and sounded with less energy utilized. I complemented her on how good she has looked after her total compliance to treatment and precautions. Her breakfast was Lipton with milk and bread. Vital signs were checked and recorded at 6:00am as;
Blood Pressure: 150/110mmHg
Pulse:76bpm
Temperature: 36.4°C
Respiration: 21cpm
Spo2: 98
During ward rounds at 10:00am, Mrs. T.t, gave no complaints when she was asked, the medical team then encourage her to continue with the previous medications without any new additions. She asked them about the possible discharge date since she felt had made a substantial progress in her recovery process, but she was told to have patience since she is still under monitoring and if her condition continues to improve, she would be discharged home in no time.
Day six Of Admission (23th August, 2023)
On the sixth day of admission, Mrs. T.t had really improved health wise. She looked really cheerful and related very well with her relatives and the other patient on the ward. She could now boldly say most of the signs and symptoms she presented with have gone. She stated she had an interrupted sleep throughout the night, all activities she could hardly perform herself before were extremely conveniently carried out and expected to go home soon. She took waakye with salad and fried fish for lunch. At 2:00pm vital signs were checked and recorded as;
Blood Pressure: 140/80mmHg
Pulse: 81bpm
Temperature: 36.6°C
Respiration: 22Cpm
Spo2: 100%
A continuous health education on hypertension was rendered to her, especially stress management right now she was getting better to prevent relapsing of condition. She took her super around 5:00pm and bathed afterward. All protocols and procedures performed were documented and signed after the 10:00pm medications and vitals.
 Day seven Of Admission (24th August, 2023)
On this day, Mrs. T.t woke up around 6:00am; she was absolutely healthy and strong. She recorded a blood pressure of 130/90 at 6:00am which spelled out the substantially depreciation of her blood pressure into normal ranges. All due medications were administered as prescribed, she observed her personal hygiene without any difficulties and took her meal around 7:00am.
Around 10:00am, during review, physician in charge of her assessed her fitness level and stability of condition. He saw the massive improvement and was even impressed; he then informed her that she was now strong enough to be discharged home for further treatment. Mrs. T.t embraced the information with so much joy and was looking forward to leave the ward as soon as possible. Emphasis was laid on adherence to medications, intake of low sodium and cholesterol diets, alcohol abstinence and management of all kind of stressful situations so her condition will continue to improve and maintain an optimal blood pressure without complications even though, the condition cannot be completely eradicated.  She was also encouraged to come for review on the 31st August, 2023 for further assessment of the condition. After settling all her medical bills, at 12:00pm, the objective set on 18th August 2023 to relieve her from dizziness and prevent her from falls was evaluated. Goal was completely met as Mrs. T.t verbalized the absence of dizziness and never fell throughout her period at the ward. Again, on 20th August, 2023, an objective was set to help patient maintain optimal peripheral tissue perfusion throughout the hospitalization period.  This objective was evaluated and indeed it was absolutely met as Mrs. T. T had a capillary refill time less than 3 seconds. At 2:00pm, prescribed medications (Tab Nefidipine 30mg and Tab paracetamol 1g) were administered and she and the family were educated on how they were going to be taken. Recording of patient’s discharge was done into the admission and discharge book and daily ward state. She was assisted to gather her belongings and was escorted to the exit. Bed was carbolized and bed side locker was disinfected.
Preparation Of Patient/Family Towards Discharge And Rehabilitation
Discharge planning started on the very of admission that is 18th August, 2023. Mrs. T.t and her family were informed that hospital would be a temporal environment which she requires for a professional caregiving to help stabilize her condition and improve her overall wellbeing, which she would be discharged home when fully fit and strong. They were reassured that, they are in the safest hands and measures would be put in place to speed her recovery. On 24th August, 2023, during review, she was informed that she was now strong enough to be discharged home for further treatment. A thorough education about medication adherence, intake of low sodium and cholesterol diets, alcohol abstinence and management of all kind of stressful situations so her condition will continue to improve and maintain an optimal blood pressure. Nevertheless, emphasis was laid on attending of follow-up review scheduled on the 31st August, 2023 for further assessment of the condition.

chapter: Chapter Four: Implementation
heading: 4.3 Follow Up / Home Visit / Continuation Of Care
text:
4.3 Follow Up / Home Visit / Continuation Of Care
Home visit encompasses the visitations made to residence of patient to assess the patient's community and identify possible risk factors that could have contributed to her current condition, offer guidance, assess progress and ensure that the patient is managing her condition or recovery effectively at home. These visits are essential for monitoring the patient's health and well-being, addressing any concerns or complications, and promoting continuity of care.
First Home Visit (20th August 2023)
The first home visit was embarked on Sunday 20th August, 2023 at 11:00am, while she was still on admission. After miss PO had visited her in the morning, I decided to follow her to her house at Yawhima. We went by a taxi which was a fifteen munities drive from the hospital. On arrival, I was warmly welcomed, offered a seat and served with a glass of water. The purpose of the home visit was to assess the environment she resides with her family to elicit factors that may interfere with Mrs. T.T’s recovery so that it would inform me about the kind of health education to provide and to locate the nearest community health facility for possible referrals after discharge. The community has social amenities like electricity, public toilet, portable sources of water like pipe-borne and boreholes. Upon entering the house, I observed the environment and it was clean, with no bushes around. Mrs. T.T and family live short building with 2 bed rooms, hall, kitchen, a toilet facility and one bathhouse built with concrete blocks, roofed with aluminum sheets plastered and painted violet and white with electricity and  pipe-borne water available. The house was built by her deceased husband and numbered YH81/3. They have a dust bin big enough to contain the refuse they make which is evacuated from time to time. I encouraged them to continue with maintenance of good personal hygiene, advice was also given on lifestyle modification and the need to comply with dietary restriction. Miss PO was thanked for welcoming me warmly; I then sought for permission to leave and promised her of my next visit.
Second Home Visit
The second home visit was made on 27th August, 2023, to assess her recovery progress in respect to the treatment following her discharge. I arrived around 10:00am and Mrs. T.T was relaxing in a sofa in the hall. She was so excited to see me again, welcomed and offered me a seat beside her. Upon assessment, there had been a significant improvement in her condition as she looked and better than during the days of admission. I encouraged her to continue taking her medication and advised her to never stop taking the medications even if she feels she had fully recovered and show no signs of the condition. Also, I reinforced teachings given earlier which include; consumption of low sodium and cholesterol foods, management of stressful situations, avoidance of alcohol and indulgent in tolerable activities and exercises. I then prepared patient and family psychologically towards my intension to hand her and the family to a public health nurse who will take charge of her during my next visit. Mrs. T.t and family were reminded on the review date which was on the 31st, August, 2023. Permission was sought to take my leave at 12:00pm of which miss P.O escorted me to the roadside where I took a taxi back home.
Day Of Review (31st August, 2023)
Mrs. T.T reported to Bono Regional Hospital at 8:30am accompanied by Miss P.O, her hospital card and health insurance were gotten for validity. After 35minutes of waiting, she was finally attended to and assessed. Vital signs were checked and recorded as;
Blood Pressure: 130/80mmHg
Pulse: 80bpm
Temperature: 36.5°C
Respiration: 20Cpm
Spo2: 99%
Upon assessment, no health issues about her condition was identified neither did she have complains. She was then advised to adhere to medication regimen and lifestyle modification in order to maintain a healthy living. She was also encouraged to be visiting the hospital when not feeling well and for regular check-ups.
Third home visit (7th August, 2023)
The third home visit was undertaken with aim of evaluating the progress she has so far made on her condition, encouraging her to comply with treatment and instructions, involving the public health nurse into her monitoring and terminating care. I got to the house at 11:30am for the last home visit and was utterly impressed with both how well Mrs. T.t was doing and my reception. Fufu with “light-soup” was prepared and served to me. Environment was tidy as expected, she continued to progress in her condition and gave no complains. She had resumed work and been active lately. The need to comply with medication, reduction in cholesterol and salt intake and regular exercises was reinforced. She also advised to desist from self-medication and duly attend to hospital for medical treatment and checks-ups. After some moment, I let Mrs. T.t and family understand the need to terminate care and promised to constantly reach out to them to know how she is doing. They were absolutely thankful for the total commitment I showed and playing a crucial role in her recovery. In return, I thanked them for their cooperation and support which enabled me to carry out this study successfully to the end. She was then handed over to the public health nurse at the nearest facility to continue with care.

chapter: Chapter Five: Evaluation Of Care
heading: Introduction
text:
Introduction
Evaluation is a critical component of the nursing process that involves assessing and appraising the effectiveness and outcomes of nursing care provided to patients (Berman et al, 2016). It is a systematic and ongoing process through which nurses collect, analyze, and interpret data to determine the impact of nursing interventions on a patient's health and well-being. Nursing evaluation helps in making informed decisions, adjusting care plans, and ensuring that the patient's needs are met effectively.
Statement Of Evaluation
Mrs. T.T was admitted on the 18th august, 2023, a thorough health assessment was done on her to identify abnormalities and deviations. Headache, dizziness, palpitation, general body weakness and anxiety were the problems or findings identified, which called for a plan of care incorporated with set of interventions to be carried out, objectives to be achieved and criteria to measure the effectiveness of the care rendered, in all to improve patient health and wellbeing. The following outlines the evaluations
Mrs. T.T Was Relieved Of Dizziness And Prevented From Falls
At 8:00pm on 18th August, 2023, Mrs. T.T was complained of dizziness, appropriate nursing diagnosis of risk for fall related to dizziness was formulated. An objective of dizziness relief and fall prevention were set to be achieved throughout the time she stays at the ward. To attain this goal, bed wheels were locked to avoid skidding of the bed to cause her to fall. Side rails her of bed were raised to protect her from falling off. She was also assisted in performing basic self-care activities such as bathing, ambulation and others. Prescribed tab Nefidipine was administered to tackle and obliterate dizziness as a result high blood pressure. Continuous implementation of the above interventions ensured Mrs. T.T got relived of dizziness and prevented from falls throughout her hospitalization period till discharge date that is 24th august, 2023 at 12:00pm.
Mrs. T.T Was Relieved Of Pain
On the 18th august, 2023 at 9:30pm, Mrs. T.T complained of severe headache, after assessment, acute pain (headache) related to cerebrovascular resistance was the appropriate nursing diagnosis formulated for the problem. An objective was set to eliminate pain from patient within the next 24 hours. The intensity of pain was assessed using the numeric pain rating scale which rating of 8/10 was recorded.  She was provided with diversional therapy by engaging her in an interesting conversation. Again, she was encouraged to have enough rest, wrapped ice cubes was applied to her forehead to relieve headache. Blood pressure was monitored four hourly to early detect and intervene abnormally increasing blood pressure. Tab paracetamol 1g was administered to relieve headache. At 10:00am on 19th august, 2023 Mrs. T.T verbalized the absence pain.
Mrs. T.T Was Relieved Of Anxiety
On 18th August, 2023 at 9:45am Mrs. T.T appeared anxious, when she was asked she clearly stated she is does not know if she can regain her wellbeing after treatment, thereafter, anxiety related to unknown outcome of condition was diagnosed. An objective to relief her anxiety was set to be achieved within the next 24 hours. Appropriate nursing interventions carried out were; Patient/family was reassured that she will regain good health with appropriate interventions, Every procedure carried on the patient was explained, All question asked by patient and relatives were tactfully and honestly answered, Patient/family were encouraged to allay all fears and concern about condition and treatment and Patient was informed hypertension get worse with stress and overthinking. After successful intervention objective were evaluated on 19th August, 2023 at 7:30pm and goal was fully met as patient appeared cheerful in bed.
Patient Regained Her Normal Sleeping Pattern
On 19th August, 2023 at 9:00am, Mrs. T.T complained she has not been sleeping well since she was admitted. A nursing diagnosis of insomnia related to change in environment was formulated. A regain of good and appreciable amount and quality of sleep as an objective was set to be achieved within 48 hours. The developed nursing interventions to combat the insomnia were; Patient was told that proper measures would be put in place to enhance her sleep, simple bed without creases and crumps was provided to her, a quiet environment was ensured, Patient was assisted to take warm bath before going to bed and Visited were restricted during sleeping hours. The implementation of these interventions was not in vane since Mrs. T.T stated on 21st August 2023 at 6:00am that she had had good sleep the last two nights.
Mrs. T.T Was Able To Perform Basic Activities Of Daily Living
On 19st August, 2023 at 11:00am, Mrs. T.T could hardly perform basic activities like grooming. A nursing diagnosis of activity intolerance related to general body weakness, an objective to aid her perform these activities was set to be achieved in the next 48 hours. Applicable nursing interventions implemented to achieve this goal were; patient nutritional status was assessed with BMI, patient was educated on nutritional meals available, patient was assisted to groom herself every morning, patient was encourage to do best they can, rest schedules were developed for patient, Patient was engaged in performing range of motion exercise and assistive devices like walkers were provided to patient to ambulate. On 21st August, 2023 at 9:00am, after the implementation of the above interventions, objective was evaluated and goal was fully met as patient verbalized that she can now perform basic activities with ease.
Mrs. T.T Maintained Adequate Peripheral Tissue Perfusion.
On 20th August, 2023 at 7:30am, Mrs. T.T was diagnosed of risk for ineffective peripheral tissue perfusion related to increased peripheral resistance because of the abnormal increased in her blood pressure, an objective to maintain the a normal peripheral tissue perfusion was set to be achieved throughout the period of hospitalization. The set of interventions implemented to attain this goal were; Peripheral pulses, capillary refill, skin color, and temperature were regularly assessed to monitor changes in tissue perfusion, Patient's extremities were elevated as appropriate to reduce venous stasis and improve blood flow, Blood pressure was continuously monitored for any significant changes, Patient was encouraged and assisted with mobility, such as regular ambulation to prevent venous stasis and promote circulation, Patient was educated about risk factors for impaired tissue perfusion, including smoking, obesity, and sedentary lifestyle, Prescribed Tab hydralazine 50mg was administered to improve peripheral blood flow. On 24th August, 2023 at 12:00pm, Mrs. T.T had no digital clubbing and a capillary refill time less than 3sec during her discharge; therefore goal was fully met when evaluated.
Mrs. TT And Family Acquired Sufficient Knowledge On Hypertension
On the 20th August, 2023 at 11:45am patient and family had little knowledge on disease condition. Upon assessment, a nursing diagnosis of knowledge deficit related to inadequate exposure to information about hypertension. An objective was set to help the patient acquire sufficient knowledge about the condition within six hours. Interventions carried out include the following; Client and relatives were assured that all discussions will be confidential, level of understanding of client and relatives was assessed by asking them questions about hypertension, adequate amount of information about hypertension was given to patient and family, a text literature of hypertension was provided to patient and relatives and Patient and relatives were encouraged to ask questions. Objective was evaluated on the 20th August, 2023 at 5:00pm and goal was fully met as nurse scored patient/family 8/10 in the post test conducted for them.

chapter: Chapter Five: Evaluation Of Care
heading: 5.2 Amendment Of Nursing Care Plan
text:
5.2 Amendment Of Nursing Care Plan.
No amendments were made in the care plan written for Mrs. TT and her family. All goals set were achieved on the allocated time due to competent nursing care and the support and cooperation received from patient family and other healthcare team.
Termination of care.
Termination of care is the ending of care and the therapeutic relationship between patient, relatives and the nurse. Since separation can bring about anxiety and depression, a gradual psychological preparation from day of admission to discharge was initiated. Mrs. TT and family were told that, hospitalization was a temporal measure to improve the patient’s condition and then they will be discharged home and handed over to a public health nurse to continue with care. Termination of care is a very difficult step to undertake but very essential. The very faithful day I started my interactions with Mrs. TT and family, I made them aware that my interactions with them will be for a short period of time. That is from admission through the period of hospitalization till discharge and then her follow up visits. After her issues were addressed, Mrs. T.T and her family were introduced to a public health nurse on my third home visit. She was pleased to corporate with the community health nurse and report to the clinic whenever she detects an abnormality. Mrs. TT and family were told to practice the health education given to them even after discharge. I also stressed on the need for lifestyle modification to Mrs. TT. She was also told to abide by dietary restrictions effectively to control her blood pressure. She was also urged to adhere to her medications and avoid the use of over the counter medications.
Summary And Conclusion
Mrs. T.T is a fifty-four year old woman who was admitted in the female medical ward at bono regional hospital through the emergency and accident unit on 18th August, 2023 with the diagnosis of hypertension.  The problems identified during the period of hospitalization included, severe headache dizziness, general body weakness, palpitation, insomnia, and inadequate knowledge about hypertension. A nursing diagnosis with objectives were developed for each problem, appropriate nursing orders were set and implemented. The objectives set were fully met with competent nursing care and cooperation from patient and family. Routine nursing care such as reassurance, provision of calm environment, checking and recording of vital signs, administering medication, serving of meal, personal hygiene maintenance and education were rendered during the period of hospitalization. Anti-hypersives and analgesics were the treatment and medications used to stabilize her condition. After a successful 7-day management of Mrs. T.T, her condition improved and she was discharged on 24th August, 2023. She was encouraged to attend reviews after discharge. Follow-up home visits were embarked on three different occasions, which was done to continue to monitor her compliance to medications and instructions given during her discharge and the improvement of her overall wellbeing. The last home visit took place on 12th September, 2023, which she looked very healthy and when asked she affirmed that, she had now regained her full strength and had now resumed her work. She was then told that, now that she had been successfully managed, she will not be regularly seeing me around anymore but I gave her my word that from time to time I will be calling to check up her, which was difficult for her to accept but she eventually did and successfully, care was terminated.
Conclusion
The study has broadened my understanding and knowledge on the predisposing factors, causes, signs and symptoms, treatment, prevention and complications of hypertension. The study has also given me the opportunity to pragmatically apply the knowledge that I have acquired. Nonetheless, through the study, I have been able to build a strong interpersonal relationship with the patient/family and the staff of Bono Regional Hospital particularly the female’s medical ward. Although the study was challenging initially, however, the experience and the knowledge I have gained will enable me to render a quality care to patients with hypertension and even with other conditions when I get to the field as a certified nurse.

PREFACE
The patient care study is a detailed account of nursing care carried on a particular patient with a specific condition at a particular time to meet his or her physical, psychological, spiritual and socio-economic needs to help him or her to attain an optimum nursing care.
Nursing has undergone much improvement over the years. It owes much of its body of knowledge to the influence of Florence Nightingale (1820-1910), a woman who pioneered and brought nursing much respect to the profession through her vision.
Nursing has basically moved from taking care of the sick to extending care to include the family members and the community in general through the use of scientific methods and techniques which are employed to help solve problems.
The patient/family care study serves as a partial requirement by the Nursing and Midwifery Council of Ghana for the award of the Registered General Nursing Certificate. It is in this regard that I chose a patient with Hypertension for the care study. The challenges I faced was financial constraints, which was managed by the financial supports from my parents.
This study helps the student nurse to get a detailed knowledge on the causes, incidence, pathophysiology, clinical manifestations, diagnostic investigation, treatments, and complications of the disease condition.
This care study has enable me to study the disease condition and offer a holistic nursing care. To ensure that confidentiality is attained, patient/family names were stated in initials instead of using their names in full. Hence Mrs. L.K is used throughout the care.
