heading: 1.9 Literature Review
text:
1.9 Literature Review
Literature review of a condition is the searching, reading, finding and synthesis of facts and results of the said condition from a previous work or study pertinent to the condition under review. It also entails seeking out for the definition, causes, pathophysiology/pathogenesis, medical and nursing managements available and other relevant information about the condition.
Sickle Cell Disease
Sickle Cell Disease (SCD) is a group of inherited blood disorders characterized by abnormal hemoglobin molecules in the red blood cells. These abnormal hemoglobin molecules cause the normally flexible, disc-shaped red blood cells to become rigid and take on a crescent or sickle shape under certain conditions (Kato et al, 2018,).
Incidence
“Approximately 5% of the world’s population carries trait genes for haemoglobin disorders, mainly, sickle-cell disease and thalassaemia. Over 300 000 babies with severe haemoglobin disorders are born each year.” (WHO, 2022).
Types of Sickle Cell Disease
With reference to Kato et al 2018, the following are the various types of sickle cell disease.
Hemoglobin SS Disease (HbSS): This is the most common and severe form of sickle cell disease. Individuals with two copies of the abnormal HbS gene (one from each parent) have HbSS. This form of sickle cell disease is often referred to as "sickle cell anemia."
Hemoglobin SC Disease (HbSC): People with one HbS gene and one HbC gene inherit HbSC. This type is less severe than HbSS but can still lead to significant health problems.
Hemoglobin Sβ0 Thalassemia (HbSβ0): In this form of sickle cell disease, individuals inherit one HbS gene and one beta thalassemia gene with no beta globin production (β0). This leads to a more severe clinical presentation.
Hemoglobin Sβ+ Thalassemia (HbSβ+): Here, individuals inherit one HbS gene and one beta thalassemia gene with reduced beta globin production (β+). This form tends to be milder than HbSβ0.
Pathophysiology Of Sickle Cell Disease
Sickle cell disease is caused by a point mutation in the HBB gene, which encodes the beta-globin subunit of hemoglobin. This mutation results in the substitution of valine for glutamic acid at the sixth position of the beta-globin chain, leading to the formation of hemoglobin S (HbS). HbS has a tendency to polymerize under conditions of low oxygen tension, leading to the formation of long, rigid fibers within the red blood cells. This causes the normally biconcave-shaped red blood cells to take on a sickle shape. The sickle-shaped red blood cells are less flexible than normal ones and can become trapped in small blood vessels, leading to vaso-occlusion. This blockage of blood flow can cause tissue damage and painful crises. The rigid HbS-containing cells are also more fragile and prone to breaking apart, resulting in hemolysis (destruction of red blood cells). This leads to anemia and the release of hemoglobin into the bloodstream. The combination of hemolysis and reduced red blood cell lifespan results in chronic anemia in individuals with sickle cell disease. Vaso-occlusion and reduced oxygen delivery to tissues can lead to ischemia (lack of blood flow) and tissue damage. This can affect various organs and systems, leading to a range of clinical complications such as acute chest syndrome, stroke, and pain crises. The damaged spleen in individuals with sickle cell disease makes them more susceptible to infections, particularly by encapsulated bacteria. The repeated episodes of tissue ischemia and reperfusion in sickle cell disease can trigger an inflammatory response, further contributing to tissue damage and complications (Kato et al, 18).

Sickle Cell Crises
According to kato et al 2018, Sickle cell crises are acute and often painful episodes that occur in individuals with sickle cell disease (SCD). These crises are characterized by the sudden onset of severe pain and can be triggered by various factors, including dehydration, infection, stress, and low oxygen levels. There are several types of sickle cell crises each with its distinct features and underlying mechanisms. The following are the various mild to life threating sickle cell crises;
Vaso-Occlusive Crisis: These are the most common type of crises in SCD. They occur when sickle-shaped red blood cells block small blood vessels, leading to tissue ischemia and severe pain. Vaso-occlusive crises can affect various organs and tissues, including bones, joints, and the spleen.
Hemolytic Crisis Hemolytic crises occur when there is an accelerated destruction of red blood cells, which can be triggered by various factors such as infections, oxidative stress, or certain medications leading to anemia, jaundice (yellowing of the skin and eyes), and fatigue.
Aplastic Crisis: Aplastic crises result from a temporary decrease in the production of red blood cells due to infection, often caused by parvovirus B19. This can lead to a sudden drop in hemoglobin levels, causing anemia and fatigue.
Sequestration Crisis: Sequestration crises involve the sudden pooling of a large number of sickle cells in the spleen or liver, leading to organ enlargement and potential life-threatening complications. In this crisis, blood becomes trapped in the spleen or liver, causing sudden enlargement and a drop in hemoglobin levels, which can be life-threatening.
Acute Chest Syndrome: A condition similar to pneumonia, characterized by chest pain, fever, cough, and difficulty breathing. It can be life-threatening.

Acute Chest syndrome
Acute Chest Syndrome (ACS) is a serious complication primarily seen in individuals with sickle cell disease (SCD), particularly sickle cell anemia. It is characterized by sudden onset of chest pain, fever and difficulty in breathing etc., which can progress rapidly to acute respiratory failure (Jain S, Bakshi N, Krishnamurti L., 2017). It occurs when red blood cells become sickled, leading to their accumulation in the terminal blood vessels of the lungs. This can result in severe chest pain, difficulty breathing, and decreased oxygen levels in the blood. Acute chest syndrome is considered a medical emergency because it can lead to significant lung damage and even death if not treated promptly.
Incidence Of Acute Chest Syndrome
“Acute chest syndrome is the commonest acute pulmonary disorder in patients with sickle cell disease. Fifty percent of patients with sickle cell disease will have one episode of acute chest syndrome. The peak incidence of acute chest syndrome is in pediatric-patients age 2 to 4 years. Within the adult population, 78% of acute chest syndrome episodes are secondary to vaso-occlusive pain episodes. Acute chest syndrome is the most common cause of death among patients with sickle cell disease accounting for close to 25% of deaths. Adults with acute chest syndrome have a 4.3% death rate, while children have a 1.1% death rate” (Amanda et al, 2023).
Causes Of Acute Chest Syndrome
According to Friend A, Settelmeyer TP, Girzadas D. (2023), the leading cause of acute chest syndrome is pulmonary embolism from fatty fragments or bone-marrow. In some cases, acute chest syndrome can be associated with fat embolism, which occurs when fat globules enter the bloodstream, often following bone marrow infarction or trauma. Other common causes of the condition are;
Pulmonary infections: Infections, particularly pneumonia, are a common trigger for acute chest syndrome. Individuals with sickle cell disease are more susceptible to infections due to impaired immune function and may develop acute chest syndrome in response to a respiratory infection.
Pulmonary infarction: Pulmonary infarction, resulting from occlusion of pulmonary arteries by sickled cells, can contribute to acute chest syndrome. This is more common in patients with severe sickle cell disease.
Vaso-Occlusion: The primary cause of acute chest syndrome in individuals with sickle cell disease is vaso-occlusion, where sickled red blood cells become trapped in small blood vessels within the lungs, leading to impaired blood flow, tissue hypoxia, and inflammation.
Lung cancer: Lung cancer can physically obstruct the airways, leading to impaired airflow, atelectasis (lung collapse), and impaired oxygen exchange. This can trigger acute chest syndrome by causing localized hypoxia and inflammation in the lung tissues.
Predisposing Factors Of Acute Chest Syndrome
Sickle cell disease patients with asthma are at higher risk of developing acute chest syndrome as compared to patients suffering from only sickle cell disease (Amanda et al, 2023). Some other predispositions include;
1. Hypoxemia: Hypoxemia, or low oxygen levels in the blood, can trigger or worsen acute chest syndrome in individuals with sickle cell disease. Reduced oxygen saturation can promote sickling of red blood cells, leading to vaso-occlusion and inflammation in the lungs.
2. Over Sedation during Surgical Procedures: Over sedation during surgical procedures can lead to hypoventilation, reduced oxygen intake, and impaired lung function. In individuals with sickle cell disease, this can increase the risk of acute chest syndrome due to decreased oxygen levels in the blood and potential vaso-occlusion.
3. Smoking: Smoking is a significant risk factor for acute chest syndrome in individuals with sickle cell disease. Smoking damages the respiratory system, reduces lung function, and increases the risk of lung infections. These factors can contribute to acute chest syndrome by promoting inflammation and compromising oxygen exchange in the lungs.
4. Pregnancy: Pregnancy is a hypercoagulable state, and pregnant individuals with sickle cell disease are at an increased risk of vaso-occlusive crises, including acute chest syndrome. The combination of increased blood viscosity and changes in blood flow dynamics can lead to sickling and pulmonary complications.
5. Vaso-Occlusive Crises: Vaso-occlusive crises are a hallmark of sickle cell disease and can predispose individuals to acute chest syndrome. These crises involve the painful obstruction of blood vessels by sickled red blood cells, and if they occur in the pulmonary vasculature, they can lead to acute chest syndrome.
6. Sickle Cell Anemia: Sickle cell anemia itself is the primary risk factor for acute chest syndrome. The genetic mutation responsible for sickle cell disease results in the production of abnormal hemoglobin, leading to red blood cell sickling, increased blood viscosity, and vaso-occlusion, particularly in the lungs.
7. Diabetes Mellitus: Diabetes can exacerbate acute chest syndrome in individuals with sickle cell disease. Diabetes can affect blood vessels and promote atherosclerosis, increasing the risk of vaso-occlusive events in the pulmonary vasculature.
8. Pulmonary Edema: Pulmonary edema, the accumulation of fluid in the lungs, can reduce oxygen exchange and trigger acute chest syndrome. Factors such as heart failure, fluid overload, or severe infections can lead to pulmonary edema.
9. Cold Conditions: Cold conditions can cause vasoconstriction and increase the risk of vaso-occlusive crises in individuals with sickle cell disease. Cold-induced pain can lead to shallow breathing and decreased oxygen intake, predisposing to acute chest syndrome.
Top of Form
Pathophysiology Of Acute Chest Syndrome
Acute Chest Syndrome predominantly occurs in individuals with sickle cell disease, a genetic disorder characterized by the presence of hemoglobin S (HbS). Hemoglobin S causes red blood cells to take on a rigid, sickle shape under certain conditions. Sickling of RBCs is triggered by various factors, such as low oxygen levels, dehydration, or infection. These sickled RBCs are less flexible and prone to sticking together, leading to vaso-occlusion. Sickled RBCs clump together and obstruct small blood vessels, including the pulmonary vasculature within the lungs. This vaso-occlusion reduces blood flow to specific areas of the lungs, resulting in localized ischemia (insufficient oxygen supply). Ischemia in the lung tissue causes hypoxia, where cells receive inadequate oxygen. Hypoxia and tissue damage prompt the release of inflammatory mediators, such as cytokines and leukotrienes, attracting white blood cells (neutrophils) to the affected areas. Neutrophils, part of the immune response, become activated. They release enzymes and reactive oxygen species, contributing to further lung tissue damage. Inflammatory mediators and tissue damage increase the permeability of capillaries within the lungs. This allows fluid, proteins, and white blood cells to leak into the air sacs (alveoli), causing pulmonary edema (fluid accumulation in the lungs). As fluid and cellular debris accumulate in the alveoli, the air sacs become filled and consolidated. This disrupts the normal exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide, exacerbating hypoxia. The pathophysiological changes result in clinical symptoms of acute Chest Syndrome, including severe chest pain, shortness of breath, fever, cough, wheezing, cyanosis (bluish skin discoloration), increased respiratory rate, fatigue, and, in severe cases, confusion or altered mental status. Left untreated, acute Chest Syndrome can progress to severe respiratory distress, acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS), respiratory failure, and can be life-threatening (Krishnan, S., Setty, Y., & Betal, S. G., 2019).
Signs And Symptoms Of Acute Chest Syndrome.
According Jain et al (2017), clinical presentation of acute chest syndrome include;
Chest Pain: Severe, sudden-onset chest pain is often the hallmark symptom of acute chest syndrome. It can be sharp, stabbing, or aching in nature and is usually located in the chest or back.
Shortness of Breath: Patients with acute chest syndrome may experience difficulty breathing, rapid breathing, or increased work of breathing. This is a result of impaired oxygen exchange in the lungs.
Fever: A high fever is a common accompanying symptom of acute chest syndrome and is often an indicator of inflammation or infection within the lungs.
Cough: A persistent, often productive cough can develop as a result of lung inflammation and the presence of fluid or mucus in the airways.
Wheezing: Wheezing, or a high-pitched whistling sound when breathing, can occur due to narrowing of the airways and increased resistance to airflow.
Cyanosis: As oxygen levels in the blood decrease, patients may develop cyanosis, a bluish discoloration of the lips, nail beds, and skin, indicating inadequate oxygenation.
Increased Respiratory Rate: Patients with acute chest syndrome often have an elevated respiratory rate as the body tries to compensate for reduced oxygen levels by breathing more rapidly.
Fatigue: Generalized weakness and fatigue can result from the body's struggle to obtain sufficient oxygen, leading to reduced energy levels.
Pain Crisis: Some individuals with acute chest syndrome experience a concomitant pain crisis in addition to chest pain. This can involve pain in bones, joints, or other parts of the body.
Confusion or Altered Mental Status: Severe hypoxia can affect the brain, leading to confusion, altered mental status, or even loss of consciousness in severe cases.
Top of Form
Diagnostic Investigations Of Acute Chest Syndrome
Chest X-ray: A standard chest X-ray is typically the initial diagnostic test to assess lung and chest cavity abnormalities, including areas of consolidation, atelectasis, and pleural effusion.
Complete Blood Count (CBC): A CBC with differential can reveal changes in white blood cell count, hemoglobin levels, and platelet count. Elevated white blood cell count and a higher proportion of immature red blood cells (reticulocytosis) may indicate acute chest syndrome.
Arterial Blood Gas (ABG) Analysis: ABG measurements provide information about oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in arterial blood, helping to assess the patient's oxygenation status and respiratory function.
Pulse Oximetry: This non-invasive test measures oxygen saturation (SpO2) and can provide real-time information about oxygen levels in the bloodstream. A low SpO2 reading is indicative of reduced oxygenation.
Hemoglobin Electrophoresis: Confirming the presence of sickle hemoglobin (HbS) is essential, as acute chest syndrome is commonly associated with sickle cell disease (SCD). Hemoglobin electrophoresis identifies the types and percentages of hemoglobin present in the blood, including HbS.
Blood Cultures: In cases where infection is suspected or needs to be ruled out, blood cultures may be collected to identify potential pathogens in the bloodstream.
Sputum Culture: If a productive cough is present, a sputum sample may be analyzed to identify infectious agents and guide antibiotic therapy.
Coagulation Profile: This set of tests assesses clotting factors and can help rule out clotting disorders or disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC), which may contribute to acute chest syndrome.
Echocardiography: In some cases, especially when severe acute chest syndrome or cardiac complications are suspected, an echocardiogram may be performed to assess heart function and identify any pulmonary hypertension.
Computed Tomography (CT) Scan: A chest CT scan can provide more detailed images of the lungs and thoracic structures, helping to identify the extent of lung involvement and rule out other conditions like pulmonary embolism.
Medical Management Of Acute Chest Syndrome
“Acute management of acute chest syndrome includes pain control, intravenous (IV) fluids, antibiotics, supplemental oxygen, and blood transfusions” (Jain et al, 2023).
Oxygen Therapy: Oxygen is administered to ensure adequate oxygenation of tissues and to correct hypoxia, a common complication of the condition.
Pain Management: Acute chest syndrome can be extremely painful. Analgesic medications are often used to relieve pain and discomfort associated with acute chest syndrome episodes.
Intravenous Fluids: Hydration is essential to prevent further sickling of red blood cells and to improve blood flow. Intravenous (IV) fluids, typically isotonic solutions, are administered to maintain or restore hydration.
Red Blood Cell Transfusion: In severe cases of the condition, where there is a significant drop in hemoglobin levels and worsening oxygen delivery, red blood cell transfusions may be necessary to replace sickled cells with healthy ones.
Antibiotics: If there is suspicion or evidence of bacterial infection, broad-spectrum antibiotics are administered to treat or prevent infection-related complications.
Bronchodilators: Bronchodilator medications, such as albuterol, may be used to alleviate bronchospasm and improve airway function in patients with acute chest syndrome.
In some severe cases, especially when there is a risk of multi-organ failure or cerebral complications, exchange transfusion may be considered. This procedure involves removing and replacing a portion of the patient's blood with donor blood to reduce the proportion of sickled cells.
For patients with recurrent acute chest syndrome or chronic lung complications, pulmonary rehabilitation programs may be recommended to improve lung function and reduce the risk of future episodes.
Platelet transfusions may be considered in cases of severe acute chest syndrome when there is a risk of bleeding or when platelet counts are critically low.
Thoracostomy (placement of a chest tube) or lung resection may be necessary to manage complications like pleural effusion or to address severe lung damage.
Nursing Management Of Acute Chest Syndrome
Observations:
Monitor the patient's respiratory status i.e. rate, rhythm, and effort. Auscultate lung sounds for wheezing, crackles, or decreased breath sounds, as these can indicate changes in lung function.
Regularly assess vital signs, including heart rate, blood pressure, and oxygen saturation. Acute chest syndrome can lead to hypoxemia (low oxygen levels), increased heart rate, and changes in blood pressure.
Evaluate the patient's pain using a pain scale (e.g., Numeric Rating Scale) to assess the intensity and location of pain. Observe for signs of discomfort, restlessness, guarding of the chest, or changes in facial expressions that may indicate pain.
Assess patient's neurological status. Observe for signs of altered mental status, confusion, or lethargy, as severe hypoxia from acute chest syndrome can affect brain function. Perform neurological checks to assess level of consciousness and pupillary responses.
Monitor fluid intake and output, especially in patients receiving intravenous fluids. Strictly monitor patient for signs of dehydration or fluid overload, such as changes in urine output, edema, or altered mental status.
Monitor vital signs during transfusion and watch for transfusion reactions.
Nutrition:
Begin by conducting a comprehensive nutritional assessment to determine the patient's nutritional status, including factors such as weight, dietary intake, and any existing malnutrition. Identify any specific nutritional needs or deficits.
Ensure adequate hydration. Patients with acute chest syndrome are at risk of dehydration due to increased metabolic demands and fever. Encourage the patient to drink fluids regularly and monitor their fluid intake and output closely.
Promote a balanced diet that provides sufficient calories and nutrients to support energy needs and tissue repair. Encourage the patient to consume foods high in protein, as protein is essential for tissue healing.
If the patient has difficulty meeting their nutritional needs through oral intake, consider nutritional supplements, such as high-calorie, high-protein shakes or enteral nutrition (feeding through a tube). Work with a registered dietitian to determine the most appropriate supplements.
Assess for any vitamin or mineral deficiencies, and provide supplementation as needed. Patients with chronic illnesses, like sickle cell disease, may have increased nutritional requirements or deficiencies that need to be addressed.
Sleep And Rest:
Coordinate nursing care activities to minimize disruptions during sleep hours. Cluster nursing assessments, medications, and procedures to allow for longer periods of uninterrupted rest.
Create a conducive sleep environment by ensuring that the patient's room is quiet, maintaining appropriate lighting (dim during nighttime), and regulating the room temperature for comfort.
Assist the patient with maintaining optimal respiratory function. This may involve administering oxygen therapy as prescribed, ensuring proper positioning (elevating the head of the bed or using pillows to support breathing), and monitoring oxygen saturation levels to ensure adequate oxygenation during sleep.
Medication:
Administer supplemental oxygen as prescribed, analgesics, antibiotics and other medications to maintain adequate oxygen saturation levels, reduce pain, prevent and treat infection to improve patient comfort and wellbeing.
Administer IV fluids as prescribed, and monitor fluid intake and output closely. Also assess for signs of fluid overload or pulmonary edema.
In cases of severe acute chest syndrome, blood transfusions may be indicated to increase the oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood and reduce sickled red blood cells.
Educate the patient and family about the importance of medication compliance and the specific medications prescribed for acute chest syndrome.
Discuss potential side effects and adverse reactions to watch for and report.
Education:
Provide comprehensive education to the patient and their family about sickle cell disease and the risk factors associated with acute chest syndrome. Explain the importance of recognizing early signs and symptoms of acute chest syndrome, such as chest pain and shortness of breath.
Teach the patient and family about the significance of maintaining adequate hydration and proper nutrition. Explain that dehydration can increase the risk of sickle cell crises, including acute chest syndrome. Encourage regular fluid intake and a balanced diet.
Educate the patient on pain management strategies, including the importance of taking prescribed pain medications as directed. Discuss non-pharmacological pain relief techniques, such as relaxation, distraction, and deep breathing exercises.
Emphasize the importance of infection prevention, as infections can trigger acute chest syndrome episodes. Encourage regular hand hygiene, vaccinations (e.g., pneumococcal and influenza vaccines), and infection control measures. Discuss when to seek medical attention for signs of infection.
Stress the importance of regular medical check-ups and follow-up appointments with healthcare providers. Regular monitoring of the patient's health can help detect and address potential issues before they escalate into acute chest syndrome.
Prevention:
Promote and ensure adequate hydration in patients with sickle cell disease. Encourage patients to drink plenty of fluids daily, especially during times of illness, exercise, or hot weather, to prevent dehydration, which can trigger sickling of red blood cells.
Proactively manage and treat pain associated with sickle cell disease. Develop individualized pain management plans for patients to reduce the risk of pain crises that may lead to acute chest syndrome.
Implement infection control measures in healthcare settings to minimize the risk of infections in patients with sickle cell disease. This includes proper hand hygiene, strict aseptic techniques during procedures, and timely administration of prophylactic antibiotics when indicated.
Ensure that patients with sickle cell disease receive recommended vaccinations to protect against infections, including pneumococcal and influenza vaccines. Keep vaccination records up to date.
Encourage a healthy lifestyle that includes regular exercise, a balanced diet, and stress management. These practices can help reduce the frequency and severity of sickle cell disease-related complications, including acute chest syndrome.
Complications
According to Amanda et al, complications to acute chest syndrome are as follows;
Respiratory Failure: Severe acute chest syndrome can lead to acute respiratory distress and, in some cases, respiratory failure. This occurs when the lungs are unable to provide sufficient oxygen to the body, leading to hypoxia
Pulmonary Hypertension: Repeated episodes of acute chest syndrome can lead to the development of chronic pulmonary hypertension, characterized by increased blood pressure in the pulmonary arteries. This condition can strain the right side of the heart and lead to heart failure.
Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome (ARDS): In severe cases, acute chest syndrome can progress to ARDS, a condition characterized by widespread inflammation in the lungs and accumulation of fluid in the air space. ARDS can lead to severe respiratory failure.
Pleural Effusion: Accumulation of fluid in the pleural space, known as pleural effusion, can occur as a complication of acute chest syndrome. This can further impede lung function and cause chest pain.
Pulmonary Infarction: acute chest syndrome can lead to pulmonary infarction, which involves tissue death in the lung due to the blockage of blood vessels by sickled cells. This can result in localized lung damage.
Chronic Lung Disease: Repeated episodes of acute chest syndrome can contribute to the development of chronic lung diseases, such as restrictive lung disease, which can affect long-term lung function.
Recurrent acute chest syndrome: Individuals who have experienced acute chest syndrome are at an increased risk of recurrent episodes. Multiple episodes can lead to cumulative lung damage and increase the risk of complications.
Cardiac Complications: Severe acute chest syndrome can strain the heart, potentially leading to cardiac complications such as heart failure and arrhythmias.
Lung Infections: acute chest syndrome can increase the risk of respiratory infections, including pneumonia. Infections can exacerbate lung damage and complicate the clinical course.
Neurological Complications: Severe hypoxia resulting from acute chest syndrome can lead to altered mental status, confusion, or, in extreme cases, coma.

1.10 Validation Of Data
Data validation refers to the process of reviewing and confirming the accuracy, completeness, and reliability of data pertinent to patients (Gil, 2023). This essential step ensures that the data used for clinical decision-making, documentation, and patient care is trustworthy and free from errors or inconsistencies. During this section, miss P.A together with her family was asked to provide answers to some relevant previously asked questions such as the onset of the crises, use of over-the-counter medication and forth. Diagnostic investigations were carried out to confirm some of the symptoms presented by her, such as conduction of chest X-ray to elicit and confirm the cause of chest pains and heaviness, Full blood count to confirm anemia due to pallor appearance etc. Data assembled from patient and family are substantial for their treatments and interventions hence they were reviewed to ensure accuracy and wholesomeness as we attempted to provide a holistic care that guarantees a complete but not partial wellness of the patient. 2.0 Introduction
Analysis is the breakdown of complex patient data or information about their health status gathered, into simpler forms to read meanings and patterns of patient problems (Daniel, 2023). This chapter presents the comparisons of information or data from the literature review pertinent to the condition of the patient and actual findings from the patient through diagnostic investigations, physical assessment etc. The analysis phase encompasses:
Comparisons of patient’s data with standards from the literature
Strengths exhibited by the patients and family
Objective and subjective health problems of the patient/family
Nursing diagnoses

Causes
Comparing the laboratory findings to the major causes of acute chest syndrome including pulmonary embolism, pulmonary infarction, lung infections, vaso-occlusion and cancer of the lung, white blood cells count was extremely high which showed Miss P.A had had pulmonary infections which had triggered the development of the condition.
Clinical Features
The clinical manifestations of acute chest syndrome outlined in the literature review have been critically compared to that presented or experienced by Miss P.A for confirmation of the condition.

Treatment

With reference from the literature, treatment modality suitable for acute chest syndrome is medical including pain control, intravenous (IV) fluids, antibiotics, supplemental oxygen, and blood transfusions.

With regards to the literature, expected or possible complications of acute chest syndrome include Respiratory Failure, Pulmonary Hypertension, Acute Respiratory Distress Syndrome ARDS, Pleural Effusion, Pulmonary Infarction, Chronic Lung Disease, Recurrent acute chest syndrome, heart failure and arrhythmias, lung Infections including pneumonia, Neurological complications such confusion, and coma.

Patient/family strength refers to the inherent abilities, resources, and resilience possessed by individuals and their families when facing health challenges or adversity (Santilli, 2018). This concept recognizes that individuals and families have unique strengths, such as social support networks, coping mechanisms, and personal qualities, which can be harnessed to improve health outcomes and enhance their overall well-being. Nursing Diagnosis
A nursing diagnosis is a clinical judgment formulated to identify potential health problems, risks, or concerns of an individual, family, or community (Ackley, 2018). It serves as the foundation for planning and implementing nursing care to improve or maintain the health and well-being of the patient or group. Nursing diagnoses for the various problems were;

4.0 Introduction
Implementation refers to the phase of the nursing process where the planned nursing care is put into action (Kozier et al, 2017). During this phase, outlined interventions and treatments in the care plan are carried out to meet the patient's needs and work toward achieving desired outcomes. It involves the practical application of nursing knowledge, skills, and expertise to provide patient-centered care.

chapter: Chapter Four: Implementation
heading: 4.1 Summary Of The Actual Care Rendered To Patient/Family
text:
4.1 Summary Of The Actual Care Rendered To Patient/Family
The delivery of the actual nursing care to Miss P.A commenced on 23rd August, 2023 which perpetuated for six days. She was vigorously assessed for deviations that compromise her health, diligently intervened to mitigate her sufferings and duly evaluated to ensure objectives set to be achieved and substantially speed her recovery are utterly met.
First Day Of Admission (23rd August, 2023)
At 3:00pm on 23rd August, 2023, miss P.A attended the paediatric unit of Bono Regional hospital through the emergency department with severe chest and back pain and difficulty in breathing. She was brought in on a wheelchair and accompanied by her mother and other close relatives. Miss P.A and her relatives were passionately attended to and welcomed. Confirmation of admission of patient was commenced by keying her Id number thus AAl7620 into the LHIMS to have access to her folder and crosscheck her details. Miss P.A and relatives were given seats to rest and wait. Soon after, an admission bed was prepared and she was put onto it and made comfortable by positioning her in a Fowler’s position in order to improve her lung expansion, capacity and improve her oxygenation. Her vital signs were checked and recorded as;
Temperature – 37.8°C
Pulse – 128bpm
Respiratory rate – 39cpm
Oxygen saturation rate – 96%
Weight – 24kg
Quick head to toe assessment was done on her and the health problems identified included; Dyspnea, chest and hip pain, fever, dizziness, coughing and pallor. Investigations requested to be carried out were full blood count, chest x-ray and pleural tap investigation. From the emergency report, she was a known sickle cell patient and diagnosed with acute chest syndrome. The following were the further treatment prescribed and planned for miss P.A during the admission period till her discharge;
IV normal saline 500mls stat
IV ceftriaxone 2g od  x 6 days
IV Paracetamol 360ml tid x 6 days
Tab ibuprofen 200mg tid x 5 days
Tab Azithromycin 250mg od x 4 days
Syrup Zincovit 10mls 0d x 4 days
IV Fluocloxacillin 600mg qid x 5 days
Tab Folic acid 5mg od  x 30 days
Tab Hyroxyurea 500mg od  x 30days
Admission procedure and other relevant information were taken and recorded in the required recording documents those are the nurses’ notes, admission and discharge book and the daily ward state. I quickly approached and greeted them and introduced myself and the name of the ward. I further orientated her mother by showing her around some of the facilities and surroundings in the ward such as the nurses’ station, washroom and others. I then introduced her and her mother to the other patient that her daughter was going to share the same cubicle with. She was then educated on the daily ward routines such as visiting hours (5:30am – 6:00am and 4:30-6:00pm), meals time (breakfast; 8:00am, lunch; 12:00pm and supper; 5:00pm) and ward rounds which mainly takes place on Tuesdays. They also learned about the vital signs monitoring hours and time medications were administered thus; 6:00am, 10:00am, 2:00pm, 6:00pm and 10:00pm every day. Finally, I conferred with her and her family the intension of embarking a project known as care study with her, which resulted in long conversation but eventually gave their consent for me to proceed.
Around 3:10pm following the arrival of miss P.A and relatives, it was no doubt she was in respiratory distress. She could hardly breathe and complained she experienced an excruciating pain at the chest the more she tried to breathe and even coughed. A suitable nursing diagnosis for the problem was formulated as; “Impaired gaseous exchange related to inadequate lung expansion”. A goal was set to help miss P.A breathe properly with ease. An objective to improve her lung ventilation was developed, so as the interventions which were going to be implemented. And they included; assisting her into a semi-fowler’s position to enhance her breathing, administering prescribed oxygen 2L/min via nasal prongs, removing all tight clothings at the chest and neck to improve ventilation, teaching her to use the diaphragm and abdominal muscle when breathing and monitoring her oxygen saturation rate to evaluate the response of interventions implemented. Again, at 3:12pm, because miss P.A complained of severe chest pain that worsens on coughing, appropriate nursing interventions such as; assessment of patient’s level of pain with Wong-Baker faces scale, positioning her properly (semi-Fowler’s) so she got confortable and did not feel pain,  administration of tablet Ibuprofen 200mg to combat pain, giving her a tablet to watch her favorite cartoons to divert her attention from pain and applying of warm compress, were planned and carried out to alleviate her of the pain. She was then allowed to have some rest before she took her supper which was rice balls with groundnut soup and chicken around 5:00pm. About two hours later, after all due medications were administered and vital signs checked, miss P.A was escorted to the washroom and assisted to bath. She looked a little tired and was allowed to have some rest. All protocols and procedures carried was documented and signed, after 10:00pm medications and vital signs.
Second Day Of Admission (24th August, 2023)
Early in the morning, at 6:00am miss P.A recorded an abnormally increased body temperature (38.1°C). She was given unrefrigerated Multifruit soft drink to consume and monitored closely for temperature change with a clinical thermometer. Again, closed windows were opened, heavy clothings were also removed and funs were turned on to improve ventilation, IV Paracetamol 260mg was administered whilst tepid sponging was done to help lower the temperature. She took “Hausa koko” with bread and milk for breakfast after a short while.
Due to vaso-occlusion, hypoxia and low haemoglobin level from the laboratory results, it was now confirmed that she was anaemic and was at risk of inadequate blood and oxygen perfusion to vital tissue which could exacerbate to even fatal complications later on if not intervened.  A comprehensive plan of care was developed to get her tissue perfusion maintained within normal levels. Interventions employed included; Assessment of mucus membranes and digits forpossible cyanosis, assisting patient into semi-fowler’s position, educating patient to avoid long stay in bed, administering prescribed IV normal saline 500mls and administering prescribed tablet Hyroxyurea 500mg all in the aim of maintaining normal tissue perfusion.
At 8:00am, it became a challenge when she had to perform her morning hygiene routine, she could even hardly walk to the washroom herself because she was very fatigued. Once this problem was detected, “activity intolerance related to general body weakness” was formulated in order to inform the development of an appropriate objective plus its relevant interventions to expedite the regain of strength so she can perform basic activities as soon as possible in convenience. She was assisted to bath, provided with ambulating assistive devices like walkers and crutches when ambulating to conserve energy, indulged in pulley and range of motion exercises, she was prevented from falling by raising side rails of bed and lowering the bed height, she was assessed of her nutritional status with a weighing scale and Body Mass Index and educated to consume high caloric and protein diet.
She requested for boiled yam with garden eggs stew for lunch. Food was ready and served to her around 12:30pm when she had had time with some of her friends and colleagues who visited her at the hospital from school; she ate about half of it and was allowed to continue her rest. At 2:00pm, due medications were administered and vital signs were checked and recorded. Soon after, range of motion exercises resumed, she was also assisted to perform tolerable ambulatory exercises around to familiarize her of the ward.
At 3:12pm, miss P.A was asked to rate the chest pains, she had the previous day on the Wong-Baker faces scale. She certainly assessed and point at 2 indicating pain had subsided to a mild degree, hence the objective set to relieve her of pain on 23rd August, 2023 was met during the evaluation.
At 6:00pm, routine medication administration and vital signs checking and recording were carried out; miss P.A’s vital signs recorded;
Temperature – 37.4°C
Pulse – 103bpm
Respiratory rate – 36cpm
Oxygen saturation rate – 98%
She was served with plain rice with tomato sauce and fish for supper, she assisted to wash down, and handed over to the night nurse after which she went to bed at 10:35pm.
Third Day Of Admission (25th August, 2023)
6:30am this day, miss P.A got up and was assisted to undertake her personal hygiene needs early in the morning. She slept very well the previous night and looked a little bit improved. She took milo with bread and milk as her breakfast, had a snappy and a quiet prayer section with her mother and return to rest. At 6:00am medications had been administered so as vital signs checked and recorded, readings as;
Temperature – 37.0°C
Pulse – 117bpm
Respiratory rate – 34cpm
Oxygen saturation rate – 98%
As vital signs particularly temperature suggested a fall in the body temperature to a normal values, the objective set to reduce high body temperature identified on 24th August, 2023 at 6:00pm, could be said to be achieved.
Around 7:45am, miss P.A was sweating proffusely and looked minimally pale as she continued to lie in bed. Her mother had complained she had refused to take in adequate amount of fluids typically water in the past days. A plan of care to outline and guide the delivery of effective care to maintain her at an optimal hydration state was drawn with a diagnosis of risk for fluid volume deficit related to sweating excessively and low fluid intake. Regular assessment and monitoring of patient hydration status, encouragement to take at least 7 glasses of water a day, regular bed rest to reduce insensible water loss from sweating, education on signs and symptoms of dehydration, such as dry mouth, dark urine and administration of prescribed IV normal saline 500mls were the crop of interventions executed to maintain her hydration status.
Around 10 am, Miss P.A together with her mother and I had a fraternal conversation about the condition and some preventive measures such as regular consumption of fluids, personal hygiene and vaccination against infections like Hepatitis A and Hepatitis B and Covid-19 among others, that she needs to adopt to ensure that she abstains from crises as possible. We also talked about the possible complications such as respiratory failure, pulmonary hypertension, pleural effusion, pulmonary infarction, heart failure, arrhythmias and coma. She complained of hunger around 11:30am, jollof rice with vegetables was the preferred meal and was truly provided around 12:00pm. She could eat an impressive amount of it and was given voltic water to consume after a short while of eating. She was then allowed to have some rest.
At 3:00pm, as miss P.A looked a bit bored, I attended to her with a story book, we read together and I asked her few questions about the story which she responded to them very well. Her father had now grown confidence and trust in me as I totally dedicated my time and energy to help make an impact in the regain of the wellbeing of his daughter. I then took the opportunity to ask him if it was possible to visit their house as I would like to undertake my first home visit. He totally agreed and expected I could do that on the 26th August, 2023 thus the next day.


Fourth Day Of Admission (26th August, 2023)
At 5:55am on this day Miss P.A woke up feeling impressively better than previous admission days, she was supported to undertake her personal hygiene activities in the morning. She appeared to have gained a substantial amount of strength and confidence since she barely needed assistance towards the washroom. She was complemented of the improvement she had shockingly made in earlier than expected. She took rice porridge together with milk and bread after due medications were administered and vital signs were checked and recorded as;
Temperature – 36.0°C
Pulse – 91Bpm
Respiratory rate – 24Cpm
Oxygen saturation rate – 98%
At 10:30am, she was made to undertake a tolerable amount of exercises to get her active by assisting her walk around the ward. She was happy she could indulge in the activity and said she would like us to have that more because she now felt stronger and better. As the activity was ongoing, I took the opportunity to encourage her to exercise as much as she can since excessive inactivity could predispose her to experience more crises but not to strain her herself or over exercise since it could also lead her to hypoxia which is equally a factor that trigger the crisis.
At 3:10pm, miss P.A was seen to have improved oxygen saturation rate, breathing with less effort and without the use of accessory muscle. These bespoke that she had improved gaseous exchange and the objective set on 23rd August, 2023 to combat impaired gaseous exchange related to inadequate lung expansion and improve lung ventilation was evaluated to be fully achieved.
She took Banku with Okro stew and beef for supper around 5:00pm, took her shower later, and had rest since she had been indulged in a lot of activities during the day. All medications were diligently administered and vital signs were checked and recorded with all other procedures documented.
Fifth Day Of Admission (27th August, 2023)
Miss P.A’s mother reported on my arrival around 8:00pm, that miss P.A nearly refused to allow her to assist her during the performance of the early morning activities including, bathing, brushing of her teeth, and visiting the toilet and even when ambulating. Surprisingly, I admired her effort so much and complimented her for the willingness and efforts made to ensure that significant progress. A review of the nursing care plan was done and an objective set to help her gain a plausible amount of strength and be able to perform basic activities on 24th August, 2023 was fully achieved.
Miss P.A took Tom-Brown with bread and milk as breakfast and resumed watching her cartoons with a tablet brought in for her. At 10:00am all medications were served and vital signs got checked and recorded as;
Temperature – 35.8°C
Pulse – 117bpm
Respiratory rate – 99%
Oxygen saturation rate – 28cpm
At 2:00pm Miss P.A and her mother questioned me about when they will be discharged because she felt very well and anticipated to be discharged home soon. I made them understand that it was of all us’ interest that she got absolutely healthy and well enough to be discharged home but since she was still improving and requires regular monitoring and check up to make sure the sickness got totally eradicated before discharge to prevent recurrence at home. She was less tensed now and promised to collaborate to ensure expedition of her recovery so she would be discharged early enough and in time that she can return to school and be in class to prepare for her end of term examination.
Supper was boiled yam with palava sauce and egg, she ate around 5:30pm, and she took her shower after and went to bed at 10:15pm. All due medications were administered with vital signs being checked and recorded plus all documentation done.
 Sixth Day Of Admission (28th August, 2023)
Miss P.A showed massive improvement in her condition on this day because she performed all her morning activities herself in convenience. She woke up around 6:00am and had been lively since. She took oats with milk and butter-bread.  Her early morning vital signs recorded read;
Temperature – 36.4°C
Pulse – 112bpm
Respiratory rate – 29cpm
Oxygen saturation rate – 98%
At 9:30am during the morning review with her physician, she assessed her vigorously to elicit if miss P.A was well enough to be discharged or continue to be on admission for monitoring for some time. She found miss P.A’s condition to be recognizably improved and could be discharged home to continue the treatment and return for review on the 13th September, 2023. It was all joyous how they have anticipated for that moment. Her mother began to contact her other relatives of concern to be ready and available for the departure from the ward. At 12:00pm, the following objectives were reviewed to be sure that interventions implemented to improve her condition were effective.
Firstly, maintenance of Miss P.A’s optimal tissue perfusion due to vaso-occlusion and hypoxia throughout her stay at the ward set on 24th August, 2023 at 8:00am was revised. Miss P.A had a reddened mucus membrane and no digital clubbing during reassessment. It was now confirmed that Miss P.A had maintained optimal tissue perfusion and definitively goal was fully achieved.
Again, due to excessive sweating and low fluid intake, an objective of maintaining her hydration status was developed on the 25th August, 2023 at 7:45am was evaluated. During evaluation, she had a good skin turgor and a moist mucus membrane indicating her hydration status was maintained at the optimum throughout the hospitalization tenure.
She together with her relatives present at this time was taken through  series of health education prior to their final exit especially compliance to and completion of medications, intake of adequate fluids, dwelling in well ventilated environment, avoidance of cold food and conditions, indulging in passive exercises and observing a good personal hygiene at home. Medical bills were taken care of due to her possession of the National Health Insurance Scheme Card and a little money paid for some other charges that NHIS card does not cover, they were reminded of the review date which was scheduled on the 13th September, 2023. She was discharged on the remaining medications she was already taking without any additions. Her name and other details were recorded into the admission and discharge book, also routines performed during the day encompassing medication administration, vital signs and other procedures were documented in the drug administration chart, temperature, pulse and respiration chart and the nursing notes respectively. All her belongings plus the remaining medications to be sent home for continuous treatment were assembled and transferred to the taxi brought in to pick them, we had our final goodbyes and they left. Her bed linen was discarded and disinfected with 5% chlorine solution, her bed and other surfaces were disinfected as well.

chapter: Chapter Four: Implementation
heading: 4.2 Preparation Of Patient/ Family For Discharge And Rehabilitation
text:
4.2 Preparation Of Patient/ Family For Discharge And Rehabilitation
Preparation of patient and family towards discharge is crucial as it can help make prediction of the duration that they can be on admission. It also establishes progress monitoring as it is compared against the expected or predicted date of discharge of patient and family.
It commenced from the admission of Miss P.A and family when they were heartened of the competent and effective care that would be rendered to promote outright regain of health and an absolute wellbeing. During the time of hospitalization, she and family were given with health education on the disease condition, its causes including pulmonary embolism, infarction and infection; the clinical manifestations such as chest pain, fever, dyspnea and possible complications like respiratory failure and pulmonary hypertension. Also an emphatic education was conducted on the following:
Nutrition:
Miss P.A and family were educated on the importance of consuming balanced diet that provides sufficient calories and nutrients to support energy needs and tissue repair, adequate fluids, fruits and vegetables, low-cholesterol diet, iron rich foods like green-leafy vegetables, high-protein foods like beans, fish etc. and vitamins especially vitamin C rich-foods like orange to help improve immune function and reduce rate of infections.
Medication:
Education about the importance of medication compliance and completion of the entire course of medications were given. Also potential side effects and adverse reactions of medications like potential low immunity linked to hydroxyurea, liver damage associated with paracetamol and bloating abdomen of folic acid were discussed with them. They were also discouraged on purchasing of over-the-counter drugs without medical order.
Prevention of complications:
Miss P.A and family were educated on the need to drink plenty of fluids daily, especially during times of illness, exercise, or hot weather, to prevent dehydration, which can trigger sickling of red blood cells. They were told to observe proper personal and environmental hygiene plus prompt vaccinations to minimize the risk and protect against infections. Regular medical checkups and attendance of reviews too were reinforced. She was encouraged to assume a healthy lifestyle that includes regular exercise, a balanced diet, and stress management to reduce the occurrence of acute chest syndrome.
They were reminded of the date of review which was scheduled on the 13th September, 2023 and informed not to hesitate to report any ailment that may occur even before the scheduled date of review.

chapter: Chapter Four: Implementation
heading: 4.3 Follow Up/Home Visit And Continuity Of Care
text:
4.3 Follow Up/Home Visit And Continuity Of Care
First Home Visit (26th August, 2023)
In the morning at 9:00am of 26th August, 2023, I embarked on my first visit to the home of Miss P.A and family as she was still on admission at the Bono Regional Hospital. The objective of this home visit was to gain insight into Miss P.A's living conditions, exploring the environmental factors that might contribute to the development or exacerbation of her condition. As I approached Abesim, place of abode of Miss P.A and family, I perceived the community to be moderately well-developed with a coal-tilled and well-constructed road. It was indeed a beautiful town with a good layout of buildings and other constructions. I followed the directions her mother gave me strictly in order to reach their house safely and timely. Upon reaching their residence with a house number of H6/16, I observed their house to be uncompleted and unpainted but kept in a clean and tidy environment from the outward. The house had two dust bins which were evacuated monthly, three bed rooms each with its toilet and bath, and sitting hall with one large LCD screen. It was roofed with an Aluzinc water proof roofing sheets and with six (6) number of people living in the house. The neighborhood seemed tight-knit, with neighbors exchanging pleasantries and children racing each other harmoniously. As I finally entered the house, I was warmly welcomed by her family, given a seat to sit and rest and served with water to drink. As we delved into conversation, I learned more about Miss P.A's daily life. The proximity of her residence to potential environmental triggers of her condition was a paramount concern. The proximity of the house to a dusty street and absence of proper ventilation in certain areas of the house raised concerns. The lack of adequate airflow could potentially contribute to the stagnation of pollutants and allergens, factors that could exacerbate her condition. Additionally, I discovered that the household relied on solid fuel for cooking, a practice known to produce indoor air pollution, which could be detrimental to Miss P.A's respiratory system. Henceforth, education was given to them about how to terminate or manage the risk factors associated with Miss P.A’s condition those were identified in the house and its environment. They were told to discourage Miss P.A from spending extended periods outdoors during peak dusty times. Family was encouraged to dampen the surroundings of their home regularly to reduce airborne dust. Use of face masks for Miss P.A when going outside, especially during dry and windy weather was recommended. Alternative cooking methods that produce fewer indoor pollutants, such as gas stove or electric cooker instead of charcoal was suggested. Also efforts to keeping windows open during the day to allow fresh air circulation was encouraged. Fans or other ventilation systems should be available, especially in areas where Miss P.A spends significant time. Happily, they consented to adhering to the teachings that was given to them; I then with a massive smile thanked them for their hospitality and cooperation after which I sought for permission to return home. I was granted with the permission and escorted to the roadside by her mother for a vehicle home.
Second Home Visit (31st August, 2023)
On August 31, 2023 around 11:30am, I returned to the residence of Miss P.A for a second home visit, following her recent discharge from the Bono Regional Hospital. The purposes of this visit was multifaceted — to assess Miss P.A’s post-hospitalization well-being, monitor the home environment for potential risk factors that can contribute to the redevelopment of her condition, reinforce medication adherence, and provide ongoing education and support. As I approached the familiar house at H6/16 of Abesim, I was greeted by the warmth of the family. The atmosphere exuded a sense of relief and gratitude, as Miss P.A's condition had improved substantially indicating a positive transition from hospital to home. I began the visit with a thorough assessment of her current health status. Engaging in open conversation with her and her family, I inquired about any changes in her symptoms and general well-being. This allowed me to evaluate the effectiveness of the recent medical intervention and identify any emerging concerns. I observed and commended the family's efforts to implement the recommended changes, such as improved ventilation and dust control measures. I revisited the importance of her prescribed medications. I mentioned the necessity of completing the entire course of medication, even if symptoms appeared to have subsided. Clear explanations were provided regarding the role of medication in preventing relapses of the condition, and any potential side effects were discussed. I reminded the family of the upcoming review date on September 13, 2023 attending the facility for medical attention when any symptom develops even before the review date. Emphases was also made on regular check-ups, underscoring the significance of the appointments to be useful in monitoring her progress, making adjustments to the treatment plan if necessary, and addressing any concerns that might arise. I took the opportunity to provide additional education tailored to her specific needs. This included discussions on maintaining a healthy lifestyle, nutrition, and strategies for coping with potential triggers in the home environment. I then unconcealed the involvement of the community health nurse during my next visit. I left the house around 12:45 after permission was sought and granted.
Day Of Review (13th August, 2023)
On Wednesday, 13th August, 2023 at 8:45am miss P.A and mother arrived at the out-patient department of the pediatrics for health assessment and evaluation of treatment so far. For a short while of waiting, she together with her mother was attended to. Her vital signs for that day read:
Temperature – 36.2°C
Pulse – 100bpm
Respiratory rate – 26cpm
Oxygen saturation rate – 99%
Vital signs corresponded to the physical and visible improvement that had occurred after her discharged. Although she looked absolutely well, emphasis was laid on the completion of the course of medications, maintenance of healthy lifestyle including consuming a balanced diet, adequate fluids, fruits and vegetables, regular activities, lowering of physical and psychological stresses that could be detrimental to her health. Miss P.A and mother were accompanied to the exit to pick a taxi to their home.
Third home visit (18th August, 2023)
At 4:00pm on this day, I embarked on what would be my final visit to the home of Miss P.A. The purpose of this visit was to confirm the full regain of her health, formally conclude our direct medical interactions, provide additional health education, and transition her care to the capable hands of the community nurse. I was warmly welcomed and provided with seat, Miss P.A had unrecognizable regained her health as evidenced by the strength with which she ran towards me to hug me upon seeing me again. They were extremely excited for how far we have kept the medical interaction. I told them how satisfied I was with Miss P.A’s progress and commended her and her family for their resilience and active participation in the healing process. I delved into further health education tailored to ensure sustained wellness. We discussed lifestyle choices, nutrition, and the importance of regular exercise. I then took the opportunity to introduce the community health nurse who would be taking over Miss P.A's ongoing healthcare needs. I provided the community health nurse with a comprehensive overview of Miss P.A's medical history, recent progress, and the strategies that had proven effective in her recovery. Before bidding farewell, I expressed my gratitude for the consent they gave me and the cooperation channeled into my project and making it a successful one and also the privilege of being a part of Miss P.A's healthcare journey. We exchanged heartfelt well-wishes, and I assured her that she was in capable hands with the community health nurse. They were equally appreciative particularly the amount of passion and dedication I put into making sure their daughter regained her health and strength. Sadly I had to bid them the final good bye since this will mark the end of our successful collaboration towards the ensuring the heath and wellbeing of Miss P.A and family. I took off from the house around 5:00pm.

chapter: Chapter Five: Evaluation
heading: 5.0 Introduction
text:
5.0 Introduction
Evaluation refers to the systematic and ongoing process of assessing the effectiveness and outcomes of nursing care and interventions implemented which involves comparing observed patient responses and outcomes with established goals and expected results to determine the success of nursing interventions (Potter, Perry, Anne, Stockert, & Hall, 2017). The evaluation process in nursing is essential for ensuring the quality of care, identifying areas for improvement, and optimizing patient outcomes. This chapter comprises of;
Statement Of Evaluation
Amendment Of Nursing Care Plan
Termination Of Care
Summary
Conclusion

chapter: Chapter Five: Evaluation
heading: 5.1 Statement Of Evaluation
text:
5.1 Statement Of Evaluation
Six nursing problems were identified during the initial assessment of Miss P.A’s, a crucial plan of care to guide the delivery of interventions aiming at optimizing her wellbeing was drawn, implementation of the spelled out interventions was carried out which now requires an evaluation or review of the care plan and comparison with patient response to confirm the effectiveness of the interventions employed.

Miss P.A Regained Adequate Lung Expansion And Optimal Pulmonary Ventilation
On the 23rd August, 2023 upon the arrival of miss P.A and relatives at the ward, it was no doubt she was in respiratory distress. She could hardly breathe. A suitable nursing diagnosis for the problem was formulated as; “Impaired gaseous exchange related to inadequate lung expansion”. An objective to improve her lung ventilation within 72 hours was developed, so as the interventions which were going to be implemented. And they included; assisting her into a semi-fowler’s position to enhance her breathing, administering prescribed oxygen 2L/min via nasal prongs, removing all tight clothings at the chest and neck to improve ventilation, teaching her to use the diaphragm and abdominal muscle when breathing and monitoring her oxygen saturation rate to evaluate the response of interventions implemented. On 26th August, 2023 at 3:10pm, miss P.A was seen to have improved oxygen saturation rate, breathing with less effort and without the use of accessory muscles. These indicated that she had improved gaseous exchange and objective set on 23rd August, 2023 at 3:10pm to help Miss P.A regain her optimal pulmonary ventilation was evaluated to be fully achieved.
Miss P.A Was Relieved Of Chest Pain
On 23rd August, 2023 at 3:12pm, miss P.A complained of severe chest pain that worsens on coughing. An objective to alleviate chest pain within 24hrs was set with appropriate nursing interventions such as; assessment of patient’s level of pain with Wong-Baker faces scale, positioning her properly (semi-Fowler’s) so she got confortable and does not feel pain,   administration of tablet Ibuprofen 200mg to pharmacologically combat pain, giving her a tablet to watch her favorite cartoons to divert her attention from pain and applying of warm compress, were planned and carried out to alleviate her of the pain. At 3:12pm on 24th August, 2023, miss P.A was asked to rate the chest pains she had the previous day on the Wong-Baker faces scale. She certainly assessed and point at 2 indicating pain has subsided to a mild degree, hence the objective set to relieve her of pain on 23rd August, 2023 was met during the evaluation.
Miss P.A Attained Optimal Body Temperature
Early in the morning on 24th August, 2023, at 6:00am miss P.A recorded an abnormally increased body temperature (38.1°C). An objective to reduce her body temperature to normal rage within 24hours was developed. She was given unrefrigerated Multifruit soft drink to consume and monitored closely for temperature change with clinical thermometer. Again, closed windows were opened, heavy clothings were also removed and funs were turned on to improve ventilation, IV Paracetamol 260mg was administered whilst tepid sponging was done to help reduce the temperature. At 6:00am on 25th August, 2023, she recorded a steady body temperature of 37.4°C which suggested a fall in the body temperature into normal values, objective set to correct high body temperature identified on 24th August, 2023, at 6:00am was achieved.
Miss P.A Had A Maintained Optimal Tissue Perfusion Throughout The Duration Of Hospitalization
On 24th August, 2023 at 8:00am, as miss P.A reported with vaso-occlusion, hypoxia and low haemoglobin level from the laboratory results a comprehensive she was suspected to be at risk of impaired tissue perfusion and a plan of care was developed to get her tissue perfusion maintained at normal levels throughout the period of the hospitalization. Interventions employed included; Assessing of mucus membrane and digits for possible cyanosis, assisting patient into semi-fowler’s position, educating patient to avoid long stay in bed, administering prescribed IV normal saline 500mls and administering prescribed tablet Hyroxyurea 500mg all in the aim of maintaining normal tissue perfusion. Evaluation of the plan was done on the day of her discharge on 28th August, 2023 at 12:00pm; Miss P.A had a reddened mucus membrane and no digital clubbing during reassessment. It was now confirmed that Miss P.A had maintained an optimal tissue perfusion and goal was fully achieved.
Miss P.A Regained A Plausible Amount Of Strength
At 8:00am on 24th August, 2023 she was very fatigued and could hardly perform basic activities. Once this problem was detected, “activity intolerance related to general body weakness” was formulated in order to inform the development of an appropriate objective plus its relevant interventions to expedite the regain of strength so she can perform basic activities within 72hours. She was assisted to bath, provided with ambulating assistive devices like a walker and crutches when ambulating to conserve energy, she was also indulged in pulley exercises and range of motion exercises, she was prevented from falling by raising side rails and lowering bed height, she was assessed of nutritional status with weighing scale and calculating her body mass index (BMI) and she was also educated to consume high caloric and protein diet. On 27th August, 2023 at 8:00am, Miss P.A required little assistance when performing the early morning activities including, bathing, brushing of her teeth, visiting the toilet and even when ambulating. An evaluation of the objective set to help her gain a plausible amount of strength and be able to perform basic activities on 24th August, 2023 at 8:00am was fully achieved on On 27th August, 2023 at 8:00am.
Miss P.A Maintained An Optimal Hydration Status Throughout The Hospitalization
Around 7:45am on 25th August, 2023, miss P.A was sweating excessively and looked minimally pale whist she had refused to take in adequate amount of fluids typically water in the past days. A plan of care to outline and guide the delivery of effective care to maintain her at an optimal hydration state throughout the hospitalization was drawn. Regular assessment and monitoring of patient hydration status, encouragement to take at least 7 glasses of water a day, regular bed rest to reduce insensible water loss from sweating, education on signs and symptoms of dehydration, such as dry mouth, dark urine and administration of prescribed IV normal saline 500mls were the crop of interventions executed to maintain her hydration status. Prior to her discharge on 28th August, 2023, the objective of maintaining miss P.A hydration status which was developed on the 25th August, 2023 at 7:45am was evaluated. During evaluation, she had a good skin turgor and a moist mucus membrane indicating her hydration status was maintained at the optimum throughout the hospitalization tenure.
5.2Amendment Of Nursing Care Plan
A quality and an effective care plan with crop of appropriate interventions were implemented in administering care to Miss P.A. It was established that all the objectives those were set to be achieved in order to ensure a timely regain of health of miss P.A were fully accomplished by the end of the evaluation. No amendments of the nursing care plan was not done as all goals set to improve miss P.A’s conditions were fully achieved

heading: 5.3 Termination Of Care

5.3 Termination Of Care
The admission of Miss P.A and family, commenced on 23rd August, 2023, through to her discharge on 28th August, 2023 and subsequent home visitation, was a profound chapter in my professional experience. The termination of our care relationship became necessary considering the fact that that she utterly regained her wellness and the need for me to attend to other equally important duties. During my last home visit that happened on the 18th August, 2023, I declared the intension of bringing our interaction to a close and instigate the community health nurse miss B.D to take charge of her to ensure continuity of care and an ongoing well-being. Also, I hammered on the need to maintain good health by indulging in all prescribed practices and education and regular medical checkups because factors like cold conditions, low ventilation, stress and malnutrition can lead to the complication redevelopment of her disease condition. As I reflect on this process, my appreciation extends to Miss P.A and her family. Their collaboration was instrumental in the success of this care study. Miss P.A's resilience was a source of inspiration, and the unwavering support from her family created an environment conducive to healing. It was not just a termination of care but a shared accomplishment in the pursuit of Miss P.A's well-being.

chapter: Chapter Five: Evaluation
heading: 5.4 Summary
text:
5.4 Summary
Miss P.A was a 10 year old girl who was sent to paediatric emergency for medical attention due to the experience of severe chest and back pain, difficulty in breathing, coughing, fever, malaise and dizziness. Upon medical assessment, she was diagnosed with acute chest syndrome secondary to sickle cell anaemia and required to be admitted and treated at the in-patient department that is the paediatric ward of Bono Regional Hospital on the 23rd August, 2023 at 3:00pm. Investigations conducted include chest x-ray, full blood count and pleural fluid analysis. Medical managements deployed to combat the condition were, IV normal saline 500mls stat, IV ceftriaxone 2g od x 6 days, IV Paracetamol 360ml tid x 6 days, Tab ibuprofen 200mg tid x 5 days, Tab Azithromycin 250mg od x 4 days, Syrup Zihovit 10mls 0d x 4 days, IV Fluocloxacillin 600mg qid x 5 days, Tab Folic acid 5mg od x 30 days, Tab Hyroxyurea 500mg od x 30 days. Significant nursing interventions employed to improve the symptoms and overall wellbeing were; assisting her into a semi-fowler’s position to enhance her breathing, improve comfort and reduce pain, teaching her to use the diaphragm and abdominal muscle when breathing, applying of warm compress on the chest to reduce pain, regular monitoring of her body temperature change with clinical thermometer, tepid sponging her to reduce high body temperature, assessment of mucus membrane and digits for a possible cyanosis, provision of ambulating assistive devices like walkers and crutches when ambulating to conserve energy, encouragement to take at least 7 glasses of water a day and regular assessment and monitoring of patient hydration status and indeed patient condition got improved and was finally discharged on the 28th August, 2023. A series of three home visits was conducted to know the condition at home and educate her and the family on proper management techniques, monitor her progress and hand care over to miss B.D the community health nurse as I needed to terminate the care on the 18th September 2023.

chapter: Chapter Five: Evaluation
heading: 5.5 Conclusion
text:
5.5 Conclusion
The culmination of the care study involving Miss P.A marks a pivotal moment in my journey as a nursing student and, more importantly, in her path to recovery. The success achieved throughout this endeavor has been instrumental in shaping not only my clinical skills but also my understanding of the profound impact of holistic, patient-centered care. The study has been a dynamic learning experience. It provided a real-world application of theoretical knowledge, reinforcing the importance of adaptability and patient-tailored interventions. It has also helped me acquire an immersive knowledge in acute chest syndrome which seemed unfamiliar from the beginning. It was a very imperative experience especially being involved in the recovery and safeguarding of miss P.A’s health not to talk about the healthy relationship that has transpired between me and miss P.A together with the entire family. In this light, I will recommend the continued emphasis on client-based care interventions recognizing the unique context of an individual's life is crucial in tailoring effective healthcare plans. Additionally, fostering strong communication and collaboration between healthcare providers, patients, and their families remains a cornerstone for achieving positive health outcomes.
